1.1: 1.1 Prologue. In Hebrew VEELLE SEMOTH, that is, THESE ARE THE NAMES; in Greek, that is, EXODUS (departure). RABANUS. In the Pentateuch Exodus excels, for in it almost all the sacraments by which the Church is instructed are expressed figuratively. For through the bodily departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, our own departure from spiritual Egypt is signified. Through the Red Sea, the drowning of Pharaoh and of the Egyptians, the mystery of baptism and the destruction of our spiritual enemies. Through the immolation of the typical lamb and the deliverance of the Hebrews, the passion of the true Lamb and our redemption. Manna is given from heaven, and water from the rock. This is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6) and the teaching of Christ. On the mountain precepts and judgments are given to the people of God, that we may be subject to heavenly disciplines. The tabernacle and its vessels are constructed, worship and sacrifices are commanded, by which the adornment of the Church and spiritual sacrifices are signified. The mystical anointing and the incense are prepared, by which the sanctification of the spirit and the fragrance of prayer are commended. Hence Paul says: All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink, etc. (1 Cor. 10). Hence also John: These things were done, he says, that the Scripture might be fulfilled: You shall not break a bone of him (John 19). BEDE. Veelle Semoth in Greek is exodus; in Latin, departure or going out.
1.5: 1.5 So all the souls that came out of the thigh of Jacob were seventy, etc. The seventy souls, that is, the seventy disciples, enter Egypt, that is, the world, with Jacob, that is, Christ, being sent, namely, to preach. Otherwise: the seventy souls who entered Egypt are understood mystically in the number of remission, so that to this age, which is figured by Egypt, after so many sins the remission of sins may be given.
1.6: 1.6 After he was dead, etc. ISIDORE, on Exodus. So, after the true Joseph tasted death for all, and destroyed him who had the empire of death, the people of the faithful was multiplied. For unless the grain had died in the ground, it would have remained alone. ORIGEN, Hom. 1 on Exodus. If Joseph dies in you, that is, if you take upon yourself the mortification of Christ, and mortify your members to sin, the children of Israel are multiplied in you, namely, good and spiritual senses. For if the senses of the flesh are mortified, the senses of the soul grow, and as the vices die in you, the virtues increase, and the land also multiplies in good works, which are carried out through the service of the body. The land had multiplied Paul, who said: But to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake. For while he remains on the earth, that is, in his flesh, the Church is multiplied by believing, by winning a people for God, and by preaching the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum.
1.8: 1.8 In the meantime there arose a new king over Egypt, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. This is the devil, who said in his heart: There is no God; who says to his own nation, that is, to the apostate angels: Behold, the people of the children of Israel, namely of those who can see God with the mind, is mightier than we: come, let us wisely oppress them. The devil perceives that the people of Israel is great and stronger than himself, because he has often engaged them and often been overcome. He knows that Jacob wrestled and by the help of an angel prevailed against his adversary, and was strong with God. He has also felt the struggles of other saints, and has endured spiritual contests; he fears lest a war should one day come, and they should join his adversaries, and, when they have been conquered [when he has been conquered], depart from his land. It seems to me, from what had been indicated to the patriarchs and prophets about the coming of Christ, that he senses that there is coming one who will strip his principalities and powers, and triumph over them with confidence and afflict them on the wood of the cross. RABANUS, on Exodus, vol. 2. We read in the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, etc., down to and perished in the Red Sea, there were many Pharaohs. ORIGEN, Hom. 1. Morally. First I want to ask who is the king in Egypt who knows Joseph, and who does not know him. For while he reigned who knew Joseph, the children of Israel are not said to have been afflicted, nor worn out in mud and brick; nor were their males killed and the females kept alive; but when he began to reign who had not known Joseph. If the Lord rules us, and the sense of our mind or soul is enlightened by God, remembering that Christ has risen from the dead, then in Egypt, that is, in our flesh, our spirit holds the kingdom with justice, and does not wear out the children of Israel, that is, the rational senses or virtues, in mud and brick, nor crush them with earthly cares. If our sense loses the memory of these things and does not know Christ, then the wisdom of the flesh, which is the enemy of God, succeeds to the kingdom; it addresses its own nation, that is, bodily pleasures, and having called the leaders of the vices to counsel, it deliberates against the children of Israel, how they may be circumvented, oppressed with mud, and afflicted with brick; how they may expose the males, nourish the females, and the Egyptians build cities and fortified cities. Nor should it be thought that the divine books narrate the deeds of the Egyptians without cause: but what was written was written for our instruction (Rom. 15), so that you who hear these things, if perhaps you have been baptized and numbered among the children of Israel, and have received the Lord as king within you, and afterwards have wished to turn aside and do the works of the world, to perform the acts of the earth and the muddy services, know that another king has risen up in you, who does not know Joseph, the king of Egypt; he himself compels you to his works, to work brick and mud; he himself, with overseers and taskmasters set over you, drives you with scourges to earthly works, so that you build cities for him; he makes you run about through the world, the seas, and disturb the elements of the earth for greed: to batter the forum with lawsuits and weary your neighbors with quarrels over a small clod of earth; to lay snares for chastity, to deceive innocence, to commit foul deeds at home, cruel ones abroad, shameful ones within the conscience; know that in such things you are serving in the army of the king of Egypt, which is to be driven by the spirit of this world.
1.11: 1.11 Therefore he set over them, etc. ORIGEN. The devil, having convened his nation, desires to oppress the rational sense, which is now figuratively called Israel: he sets over them masters of works, to force them to learn the works of the flesh, according to Psalm 105: They were mingled among the nations, and learned their works. He teaches them to build cities for Pharaoh: Pithom, which means mouth of defection, or of the abyss; and Ramesses, which is the moving of the moth; and On, that is, Heliopolis, which is called the city of the sun. The mouth fails when it speaks a lie, away from truth and proofs. He was a liar from the beginning, and therefore wants such cities built for himself: the mouth of the abyss, because the abyss is the place of his perdition; another of his cities is the moving of the moth: for whoever follows him lays up treasure where the moth consumes and thieves dig through and steal (Matt. 6). He also builds the city of the Sun, transfiguring himself with a false name into an angel of light. With these things he occupies minds that were made to see God. Yet he foresees that wars are hanging over him and that the ruin of his nation is ripe; therefore he says, The people of Israel is mightier than we: would that he might also feel that we are mightier than he: namely, that I should not accept the evil thoughts and desires which he sends in, but repel the fiery darts with the shield of faith, and in everything he suggests, say: Get behind me, Satan: for it is written: You shall adore the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve (Matt. 4). But also in what he says, Lest perhaps war come upon us, and they join our enemies, he foresees from the prophetic words that war will come upon him, and that he will be forsaken by the children of Israel, and that they will join his adversary and be added to the Lord. This is what Jeremiah says (ch. 17): The partridge has cried out, she has gathered what she did not lay: he has made riches, and not by right: in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and in his last end he shall be a fool. He understands, then, that he is the partridge who has gathered what she did not lay; and that those whom he gathered without justice will leave him and follow Christ, who begot them. He himself will remain a fool, when the whole creation has fled to its maker and parent; therefore he is indignant, saying: Lest they fight against us and go out of our land. He does not want us to go out of his land, so that we may always bear the image of the earthly one: lest, leaving him, we flee to him who has prepared the kingdom of heaven, leaving the image of the earthly and taking up the image of the heavenly. Therefore he appointed masters of works, to teach their arts and make us craftsmen of malice. And because there are many masters of malice whom Pharaoh has set over us, who command, exact, and extort earthly works: therefore at the coming of Christ he made other teachers fighting against them, who, subjecting all their principalities and powers and virtues, defend the children of Israel from violence, and teach the works of Israel, and to see God with the mind; to leave the works of Pharaoh, to go out of the land of Egypt, to put off Egyptian ways and the whole old man with his deeds, and to put on the new man, who is created according to God. ISIDORE. Israel signifies the Christian people, Pharaoh the devil, who lays upon them the very heavy yoke of mud and brick, that is, the servitude of earthly and muddy work; with straw mixed in, that is, with light and irrational deeds: so that, with all oppressed by the burden of sins, there may be no one to destroy or conquer his kingdom.
1.15: 1.15 And the king of Egypt spoke to the midwives, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 2. We find these things not only in the world, which is spiritually called Egypt, but in each one of us: the prince of this world does not want the males to be kept alive, but the females; in the woman the flesh and the affections of the flesh are designated: but the man is the rational sense, and the intellectual spirit, which can grasp heavenly things, understand God, and seek the things that are above. The prince of Egypt hates this and desires it to be killed; he desires that the things of the flesh live, and those that pertain to bodily matter, not only to live but to be increased and cultivated: for he wants all to savor the carnal, to seek temporal things and the things that are upon the earth; let no one lift his eyes to heaven; let no one ask whence he came here; let no one remember his homeland, paradise. When, therefore, you see men leading their lives in pleasures, floating in luxury, giving themselves to banquets and impurities, know that in these the king of Egypt kills the males and keeps the females alive. But if one in a thousand is converted to God, raises his eyes upward, seeks eternal things, hates delicacies and luxury, loves continence: Pharaoh desires that one, as a male, be killed; he persecutes him and assails him with a thousand devices; he hates such people and does not allow them to live in Egypt. Hence it is that in this world the servants of God are held in contempt and exposed to insults; hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them. To the midwives. ORIGEN, ibid. He also tries to corrupt the midwives. Of whom one was called Shiphrah, that is, a sparrow; the other Puah, that is, blushing or modest; through them he seeks that the males be killed and the females kept alive: but the midwives feared God, and did not do as he had commanded them. The midwives taught us before us to hold a certain form of rational learning. For midwives are physicians, and tend both males and females at birth. Common learning, then, is rational knowledge, and reaches almost every sense, instructs all and tends them. If anyone in it has a manly spirit, who wishes to seek heavenly things and pursue divine things, as one healed and strong, through these studies he would come better prepared to the understanding of divine things. For there is one, like a sparrow, which teaches higher things and calls to the heights on the wings of rational teaching; the other, blushing or modest, is moral, it arranges conduct, and teaches modesty and honorableness. To me, however, since Scripture says of them that they feared God and did not do according to the command of the king of Egypt, they seem to preserve the figure of both Testaments, and Shiphrah, which is interpreted a sparrow, to fit the law, which is spiritual; but Puah, which is blushing or modest, to indicate the Gospels, which are red with the blood of Christ, and glow throughout the whole world with the blood of the passion. By these, then, the souls that are born in the Church are treated as by midwives, because from the Scriptures all the medicines of instruction are supplied. Yet Pharaoh tries through them to kill the males, when he suggests heresies and perverse doctrines to those who are devoted to the divine Scriptures. But the foundation of God stands immovable. For the midwives fear God, that is, they teach the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. Thus what follows is more fittingly applied: because the midwives feared God, he built them houses. According to the letter this has no logical connection: for a house is not made because God is feared. But if you see how the Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, teaching the fear of God, make houses of the Church and fill the whole world with houses of prayer, it will seem reasonably written. Thus, then, these midwives, because they fear God, that is, teach the fear of God, do not carry out the command of the king of Egypt, but keep the males alive; and yet it is not said that they obeyed in keeping the females alive. And I say confidently, they do not keep the females alive. For vices and luxury are not taught in the Church, nor are sins nourished, as Pharaoh wishes when he orders the females kept alive, but virtue alone is cultivated and nourished. But let us refer these things to each one. If you fear God, do not carry out the command of the king of Egypt: for he commands you to live in delights and to covet present things; you, if you fear God and perform the office of a midwife, if you wish to bring benefit to your soul, keep the males alive, that is, you heal and tend the inner man who is in you, and through good acts and understanding you obtain eternal life.
1.16: 1.16 If it be a man child, etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. Pharaoh orders the males to be killed and the females to live: so the devil, lest the strength of faith should prevail, wishes the virtues to be killed and the vices to live, and strives to kill the strong and manly senses of the mind, by which we savor divine things, that is, reason, prudence, constancy, innocence and faith; and what is womanish, weak, fragile and prone to vices he desires to survive, that is, ambition, violence, lust, anger, and the like, which are the figure of women.
1.19: 1.19 They answered, etc. AUGUSTINE, on Genesis, vol. 3. The question is whether such lies are approved by divine authority, etc., down to but those whose conversation is already in heaven, I do not think that they ought to shape the manner of their speech concerning truth and falsehood on the example of the midwives. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 38, ch. 2, 3. Lying is to be avoided with the utmost care, etc., down to for in sparing the infants they tried to cover their lives by lying, their own. AUGUSTINE, in the book On Expressions in Exodus, vol. 3. And because the midwives feared God, etc., down to so that it seems to pertain to the very making of the house that the wages are consequently proposed to be fixed by Laban.
1.22: 1.22 Pharaoh therefore charged, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 2. The Egyptians, to whom Pharaoh here commanded that they should keep only the females alive, hated the males. For they hate the virtues and have nourished the vices. Even now the Egyptians lie in wait, if a male is born to the Hebrews, to kill him at once, unless they are on guard, watchful and hidden. Scripture relates that someone of the tribe of Levi begot a male, and saw that the child was beautiful and hid him. Let us therefore not do our justice before men, but with the door shut let us pray to our Father in secret, and let not the left hand know what the right hand does, lest it be snatched away by the Egyptians, attacked, and drowned in the waves. If I give alms because it is a work of God, I beget a male; but if I seek praise from men, and do not hide it, it is seized by the Egyptians, plunged into the river, and with so much labor and so much zeal I have begotten a male for the Egyptians. Whatever is feminine. JEROME, on Ecclesiastes, ch. 3. Wherever in the Scriptures a woman and the weaker sex are read of, let us transfer it to the understanding of matter. Hence Pharaoh does not want males to be born, but females, who are close to matter; and on the contrary, none of the saints, except very rarely, is said to have begotten daughters. And only Zelophehad, who died in his sins, begot all daughters: Jacob is the father of one daughter, and is endangered because of her.
2.1: 2.1 There went a man, etc. RABANUS, on Exodus, vol. 2. Hence Josephus says: But Amram, fearing lest he be caught and succumb to the royal wrath, etc., down to or to bring out, as Moses was brought out of the river. Allegorically. The parents of Moses, whose faith and works the natural law adorned. The same, ibid., down to she too is taught to be ashamed to worship idols. A man of the house, etc. DIODORUS. The father of Moses is passed over not without purpose: for Christ also, whose type Moses bore, is without a father.
2.2: 2.2 And seeing, etc. CHRYSOSTOM, Hom. 54 on Acts. It is wonderful that all things are done for us not through what seems to be security, but plainly through the opposite. Pharaoh ordered the boys to be cast into the river; had the boys not been cast out, Moses would not have been saved: when he was being saved, he was not in honor; when he was exposed, then he was made honored. The Jew threatened him, saying: Will you kill me too? and this benefited him, that he might philosophize in solitude and live in safety. ORIGEN, Hom. 2. Allegorically. Pharaoh's daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, to whom it is said through the prophet: Forget your people and your father's house, for the king has desired your beauty (Ps. 44). She is therefore the one who went out of her father's house and came to the waters, to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father's house: and at once she took on the bowels of mercy and had pity on the child; coming to the marsh, she found Moses lying, exposed by his own, and had him nursed. He is nursed among his own, there he spends his infancy; having grown stronger he is brought to her, and is adopted as a son. Moses signifies the law. The Church, then, coming to the waters of baptism, received the law enclosed within the ark and smeared with bitumen. The ark is a kind of covering woven of papyrus, and formed of rods or of tree bark. The law, then, lay shut within such coverings, smeared with pitch and bitumen, namely with the base and foul senses of the Jews; it lay besmeared and filthy until the Church came from the Gentiles and took it from the muddy and marshy places into the halls of wisdom and royal roofs. Yet it spends its infancy among its own: for among those who do not understand it spiritually it is little, an infant, and has the foods of sucklings: when it comes to the Church, Moses is stronger and more vigorous; for when the veil of the letter is removed, perfect food is found in its reading. He receives the wages of nursing from Pharaoh's daughter, with whom the law is born and nourished. But what is it that the Synagogue receives from the Church? I think it is what Moses says: I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will stir you to anger. The Synagogue, then, receives this wage from the Church, that it may no longer worship idols: for seeing the Gentiles so converted to God that they no longer know idols, it is ashamed any longer to worship idols. We too, if we had Pharaoh for our father, if he begot us in evil works, when we have come to the waters, let us take up the law of God: let not its letters be foul to us like an obscure covering; let us eat what is small and milky in it; let us take what is perfect, and lay it up within the royal chambers of the heart. We have a great and strong Moses: let us think nothing small or base about him, but all of him magnificent, all excellent, all elegant: for everything that is spiritual and of sublime understanding is great.
11.2: 11.2 Say therefore to all the people, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 94 on Exodus, vol. 3. No one should take an example from this, etc., down to so that those who had not been struck by the other plagues might not be smitten by this loss either. That the man ask, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 28, ch. 17. Minds clinging to the use of carnal life, etc., down to greater strength of spirit is announced.
11.3: 11.3 And the Lord will give favor to his people in the sight of the Egyptians, etc. Namely, those who lived with the Hebrews in the land of Goshen and had not been harmed by the nine plagues for their sake, and therefore loved them: they were afflicted by the tenth plague, when the Hebrews had departed from them.
11.5: 11.5 And every firstborn shall die, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 4. Last of all destruction is brought upon the firstborn, in which perhaps there is something beyond our understanding, in that what is committed by the Egyptians seems to be against the Church of the firstborn, which is enrolled in heaven. Hence the destroying angel is sent for this ministry, who spares only those who had both doorposts marked with the blood of the lamb. The firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed again: whether we call them the principalities and powers and rulers of the darkness of this world, whom Christ by his coming led away, that is, led captive and took captive, when he triumphed on the wood of the cross: or the authors and inventors of false religions, which the truth of Christ extinguished together with its authors. The principalities, and powers, and rulers of this darkness are the firstborn of the Egyptians who [other reading, which] in the last plague, namely when the end of the world has come, when he will separate the sheep from the goats, the grain from the chaff, will be condemned, having lost the license to wander and tempt. ORIGEN. Morally. The soul, while it lives in this world in errors, in ignorance of the truth, is placed in Egypt: if the law of God begins to draw near, it turns the waters into blood, that is, it turns the fluid and slippery life of youth to the blood of the Old or New Testament. Then the law draws out of it vain and empty talkativeness against the providence of God, like the complaint of frogs. It also purges its malignant thoughts, and shakes off the stings of cunning, like the biting of gnats. It also drives away the bites of lusts, like the darts of the dog-fly: and the folly and understanding like that of cattle, through which man, when he was in honor, did not understand, but was compared to senseless beasts, etc. (Ps. 48). It reproves the ulcers of sins, and extinguishes the swelling of arrogance and the heat of rage. After this it applies the voices of the sons of thunder, that is, the evangelical and apostolic teachings, and the chastisement of hail, to restrain luxury and pleasures; and at the same time the fire of penitence, so that it may say: Was not our heart burning within us? (Luke 24). It also withdraws from it the examples of the locusts, by which all its restless and turbulent motions are devoured, that it may learn to do all things in order. But when it has been sufficiently chastised for its ways, when it has felt the author of the blows, confessing that it is the finger of God, and has received a little knowledge: then especially it sees the darkness of its deeds and the gloom of its errors, and then it will deserve that the firstborn of Egypt be extinguished in it. For every soul, when it has come to the fullness of age, and as the natural law begins to defend its rights in it, produces first motions according to the desire of the flesh, which the stimulating force has stirred up from the fuel of concupiscence or anger. Hence the prophet says of Christ, as a singular privilege: He shall eat butter and honey; before he does or brings forth evil, he will choose the good (Isa. 7); for before the child knows good or evil he will resist malice, to choose what is good. But David says of himself: Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances (Ps. 24). Because therefore these first motions of the soul, brought forth according to the flesh, fall into sin, rightly in the moral sense the firstborn of the Egyptians are put as first things, because they are extinguished if the conduct of the remaining life directs a more amended course. So, then, in the soul which the divine law takes up from errors and chastises, the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed, unless after all this, persisting in unbelief, it refuses to be joined to the people of Israel, to come out of the deep and escape unharmed, but remains in iniquity and sinks like lead in the mightiest water. For iniquity, according to Zechariah (Zech. 5), sits upon a talent of lead: and therefore he who remains in iniquity is sunk like lead into the deep.
11.7: 11.7 Among all, etc. AUGUSTINE in the book of Expressions. It is a most elegant expression: by the dog he signified the lowest, either of men or of cattle: thus he emphasized how great a quiet there would be among the Hebrews, while the Egyptians cried out in bitter bereavement.
11.9: 11.9 Pharaoh will not hear you, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 40 on Exodus. As though the disobedience of Pharaoh had been needed for those signs to be multiplied: which were usefully done to terrify the people of God, and by that very distinction to form them to piety. But this was of God, who made good use of the malice of that heart, not of Pharaoh, who badly abused the patience of God.
12.2: 12.2 This month, etc. RABANUS. This is April, which among the Hebrews is called Nisan, among the Macedonians [Xanthicus]; and it is called Aprilis as if aperilis, because then the earth is opened to bring forth shrubs, herbs and flowers: or Aprilis from Venus, as if Aphroditis; for Venus in Greek is called Aphrodite. The Hebrews have this as the first, because the fifteenth day before its Kalends was the first day of the world: the fourteenth, the second day; the thirteenth, the third: the twelfth, the fourth: on which the sun and moon were made, and then was the first equinox; for the sun in the east and the moon in the west divided the sphere of the world equally. STRABO. This is Nisan, according to the Hebrews, in which the world was made, whose full moon after the vernal equinox must always be observed: in which the people of Israel is freed from the servitude of Egypt, and the human race is rescued by the blood of Christ from the power of the devil. On the tenth day of the month the lamb is taken, on the fourteenth it is immolated: because in the law the passion of Christ is figured, and is fulfilled with the grace of the Gospel shining forth; for ten, on account of the decalogue, signifies the law; four, the four Gospels.
12.5: 12.5 And it shall be, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 42 on Exodus, vol. 3. That expression can raise a question, etc., down to what is figured by that precept. According to which rite, etc. Allegorically. Because Christ took flesh from the just and from sinners, so that no one should despair of pardon. Or because Christ was a kid to the Jews, who said: This man is a sinner (John 9), but to us a lamb without spot. Or because he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh and died for sin, though he had no sin (1 Pet. 2). STRABO. On the tenth day of April he came to Jerusalem, and on the following day was received by the crowds with palm branches and divine praises. For the remaining three days he was kept by the Jews until the fourteenth day, that is, until the fifth day of the week, on which he supped with the apostles, and afterwards was handed over.
12.7: 12.7 And they shall take of the blood thereof, etc. GREGORY, Hom. 22 on the Gospels, vol. 2. The blood is placed on the doorposts when it is drunk not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart, etc., down to because we bear the cross of his passion on our forehead.
12.8: 12.8 And they shall eat the flesh, etc. GREGORY, ibid. We eat the lamb by night, etc., down to for he offers praise from leaven who prepares a sacrifice to God from plunder. With wild lettuce, etc. GREGORY, ibid. Wild lettuces are very bitter, etc., down to so that he may know that all things are dispensed by the power of the Holy Spirit.
12.9: 12.9 The head with the feet, etc. GREGORY, ibid. The head of Christ is God (1 Cor. 11). To devour the head of the lamb, therefore, etc., down to let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland. GREGORY OF NYSSA, On the Life of Moses. By those wrappings of things he warns us that through these enigmas we should wish to consider and understand that this our life is a kind of passage. For after we have entered upon it, we are always compelled by a certain necessity toward the exit, for which he wishes us to be prepared with hands and feet and the rest of the equipment for the journey. So that our feet may not be hurt by thorns on this arduous journey of living, we ought to travel not barefoot but protected with harder shoes. The thorns, which, fixed in the feet, not only hold and delay but even kill, are sins, against which the hardness of shoes defends, namely continence, a thin and hard life, which weakens and breaks the points of the thorns, by which sins, from a small and slight beginning, advance to the foremost so as utterly to kill. For making this life, a long and flowing garment, that is, a voluptuous and vicious manner of living, which spreads very widely, is an impediment: therefore it must be drawn up and restrained by a girdle, lest it flow about here and there. The girdle is modesty and a careful manner of living, which warns us to use things for necessity, not for pleasure. The staff, with which we drive off wild beasts and sometimes are supported, is hope. Only food from the fire is set before us, because faith, which is signified by that food, ought to be most ardent, possessing nothing moist or unstable. Phase. In Hebrew it is Pesach, in Greek, that is, passage; because it was first celebrated by the children of Israel departing from Egypt: we too must migrate from transitory to eternal things, from earthly to heavenly.
12.12: 12.12 Upon all the gods, etc. The Hebrews report that all the idols of Egypt and the temples were broken that night, either by an earthquake or by the flooding of the river Nile. Allegorically, as we come out of Egypt the idols of errors fall, and all the worship of perverse doctrines is shaken.
12.14: 12.14 And you shall have this day, etc. AUGUSTINE, on Exodus, Question 43, vol. 3. And you shall keep this day for your generations as a lawful, eternal or everlasting ordinance (which is said in Greek); it is not to be taken in this way, etc., down to at every time of the present life simplicity is to be kept, malice to be avoided.
12.18: 12.18 In the first month, on the fourteenth day, etc. RABANUS. Mystically. The evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, in which the Passover is celebrated and the immolation of the lamb is completed, signifies the putting off of the old man and the beginning of the new, which is begun in baptism, figuring the death of Christ. Hence: As many of us as have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized in his death, etc. (Gal. 3 [sic]). From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first, a whole week, namely, we are commanded to eat unleavened bread, because from the reception of baptism to the end of life we ought to live simply and without guile. Hence Peter: Laying aside all malice and all guile and dissimulation, as newborn babes, etc. (1 Pet. 2).
12.21: 12.21 The elders. Note that God communicates his commands first not to boys nor to young men, but to the elders, because in the aged is wisdom, and in length of time prudence.
12.22: 12.22 And a bunch of hyssop, etc. STRABO. Hyssop is a lowly herb, growing on rocks, cleansing the chest and lungs: and it signifies true humility, of which Christ gave us an example in himself. We dip the bunch of hyssop in blood when, mindful of the humility of Christ, we strive to imitate him. Dip it in the blood, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 46 on Exodus. It is asked what blood he means by the door, since he wishes the blood of that lamb to be understood by whose immolation the Passover is made. Or does he command that it be done in that way, although he was silent on it, that the same lamb be killed by the door? Or, what is more credible, did he say from the blood which is by the door because he who is to smear it will place the very vessel in which he received the blood by the door, so that he may have it at hand while he dips?
12.23: 12.23 And he will not suffer the destroyer, etc. STRABO. Whether the destroyer was a good or an evil angel need not be inquired: for whoever he was, he obeyed the command of the Lord. It should be known, however, that evil angels are wont to cause such plagues by God's permission. The tenth commandment is: You shall not covet your neighbor's goods, etc. Contrary to this is the tenth plague, the death of the firstborn. In another commandment theft is forbidden, by which robbery is also condemned: for it is worse to snatch violently than secretly. One who wishes to take away, openly or secretly, has his own commandment: but to covet the goods of a neighbor, even if you seek them by just succession, is not allowed. For those who wish to possess others' goods as though justly also look for being heirs while the owners die. When you praise a thing left behind as if possessing it by right, God condemns the unjust coveter. For you who seek to become an heir of someone do not wish him to have heirs, among whom nothing is dearer than the firstborn. Rightly, then, you are punished in your firstborn, you who by coveting others' goods seek the shadow of right, and lose what is better, the firstborn of the heart. The firstborn is faith. For no one does good in whom faith has not gone before. All good works are spiritual sons, but among these faith is the firstborn. Whoever therefore secretly covet another's goods, you lose faith within. For you serve not out of charity but out of fraud, as loving one whom you desire to die so that you may succeed.
12.30: 12.30 For there was not a house, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 44 on Exodus. Since only the firstborn died, how was there no house in which there was not one dead? Or was this also divinely arranged, that in all houses there were firstborn, in which the Egyptians would be struck, even those who dwelt in the land of Goshen? For they were here of men or of animals, not of the land; that is, the firstborn men and animals died, by a hidden and angelic blow: nothing was done in the land or in the sky, as with the frog, or locust, or darkness. For from such plagues, since the land of Goshen had been exempt, the benefit reached the Egyptians who lived in it with the Hebrews: but by this plague all were struck.
12.34: 12.34 The dough, etc. AUGUSTINE. Mystically. The children of Israel set out from Egypt without leaven; that, going out of this world, we may cast away the leaven of malice and wickedness, and feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
12.35: 12.35 And they asked, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 45. This had already been done before the deaths of the firstborn. But now it is repeated by recapitulation, for it is narrated when it was done. For how could it be done now that these things were lent in such great mourning: unless perhaps someone says that by this plague also the Egyptians who dwelt with the Hebrews were not struck. Vessels of gold, etc. These signify the doctrines which, from the very custom of the nations, are learned by a not useless study; or precious souls from the nations, like vessels of gold and silver; with garments, that is, bodies: which join themselves to the people of God, that they may once be delivered from this world as from Egypt.
12.37: 12.37 And the children of Israel set out, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 5 on Exodus. He who prepares to set out from Egypt, who desires to leave the obscure acts of the world and the darkness of errors, must first set out from Ramesses, which is interpreted the moving of the moth. If you wish to come to this, that God be your guide, and the rock follow you, giving spiritual food and drink, go out of Ramesses, do not lay up treasures where the moth destroys and thieves dig through, etc. If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me (Matt. 6 [sic]); this is to set out from Ramesses and follow Christ. From Ramesses to Succoth, etc. ORIGEN, ibid. Let us see what the place of the encampments is to which they come. From Ramesses they came to Succoth, which is interpreted tabernacles. When, therefore, leaving Egypt, you have shaken off the moths of all corruption, and cast out the incitements of vices, you will dwell in tabernacles, from which we do not wish to be stripped but clothed over. The dwelling in tabernacles indicates that he who hastens to God is unencumbered. But we must not stop even here: the camp must be moved also from Succoth, and we must hasten to Etham, which is interpreted signs to them, because here you will hear that God goes before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire; not so in Ramesses, nor in Succoth, which are the second camps. The third are those in which divine signs are made: this was the three days to which Moses and Aaron hastened, and Pharaoh contradicted saying: Do not go farther. He did not want the children of Israel to come to the place of signs, so that they could enjoy the mysteries of the third day. Hence Hosea 6: God will raise us up after two days, and on the third day we shall rise again, and live in his sight. The first day for us is the passion of Christ; the second, on which he descended into hell; the third, on which he rose again: therefore on the third day he went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire. It is necessary, therefore, that those who are baptized in Christ be baptized in his death, and be buried with him, and rise on the third day, whom he raised up with himself and made to sit together in the heavenly places (Rom. 6). About six hundred thousand, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 47. It is asked whether the Hebrews reached so great a number during those years in Egypt, etc., down to that is, after the death of Joseph they were oppressed with hard servitude.
12.46: 12.46 Nor of it, etc. The bone of Christ on the cross was not broken, because seeing him already dead they did not break his legs: or the strength of the divinity in the flesh is not corrupted by blasphemy, because he is not a mere man, but true God.
13.2: 13.2 Sanctify to me every firstborn, etc. Because I slew all the firstborn of the Egyptians for your deliverance.
13.9: 13.9 And it shall be as a sign, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 48 on Exodus. What is it that he says when he commands about the Passover, etc., down to otherwise grace would no longer be grace.
13.13: 13.13 And every firstborn of man, etc. CYRIL. He commands the firstborn of men to be redeemed, to forbid murder: for he created all things to be incorruptible. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 27, ch. 1. The ass signifies uncleanness, the sheep innocence. To change the firstborn of an ass for a sheep, therefore, is to convert the beginnings of an unclean life into the simplicity of innocence, so that, after the sinner has done those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now by his deeds bring forth things he may lay upon the sacrifice of God. For we are all born in sin, and conceived from the delight of the flesh, and have contracted original guilt. Hence also by our own will we are entangled in sins. But he too who after the malice of the flesh is converted to innocence of heart changes the firstborn of an ass for a sheep, namely the malice of his former life. For he who ceases to be what he was before, and, having taken hold of purity of the flesh, keeps innocence, has changed the firstborn of an ass for a sheep as an offering to God.
13.16: 13.16 And as a thing hanging. The Jews, understanding this wrongly, bound pittacia or phylacteries around their heads, in which they had the ten words written before their eyes.
13.17: 13.17 Now when Pharaoh had sent out, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 24, ch. 13. Often the converted, at the very entrance of their conversion, receive tranquillity of the flesh, gifts of prophecy, the sayings of doctrine, the miracles of signs or the grace of healings. Afterwards they are wearied by harsh trials of temptations, from which they believed themselves free: because if the bitterness of temptations had beaten upon them at the beginning, they would easily have returned to the vices from which they had not gone far. Therefore for those going out of Egypt wars are withdrawn from nearby: because to those leaving the world a certain tranquillity is shown first, lest, disturbed in that very tenderness and beginning, they return to what they had left: first, then, they feel the sweetness of security, first they are nourished in the quiet of peace; but after the sweetness is known, they bear the contests of temptations the more tolerably, the more deeply they have come to know in God what they love.
13.18: 13.18 God did not lead them, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 49. Here it is shown that everything that can rightly be done by counsel ought to be done, to avoid what is adverse, even when God is most openly the helper (Epistle to Damasus, vol. 1 [sic]). And the children armed went up, etc. JEROME. Aquila, who is not contentious, as they think, but careful, translates word for word; where the Septuagint put, But in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt, he translated, And armed the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt, although for what we have said armed, according to the ambiguity of the Greek language, it can be understood as equipped or fortified on account of the goods with which they despoiled the Egyptians. But where the Septuagint put fifth generation, those who have carefully examined the books of the Hebrews report that it is written not fifth but five, so that the sense is: But five of the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt; and because this seemed less intelligible, generation was added. Aquila is said to have translated literally, both elsewhere and especially in this place, as all the seats of the synagogues agree. AUGUSTINE, Question 53. But in the fifth generation, etc. Does he wish to count a generation as a hundred years, etc., down to Nahshon begot Salmon.
13.21: 13.21 And the Lord went before them, etc. ORIGEN. When the mystery of the third day has been received by you, God will begin to lead you and show you the way of salvation. GREGORY. In the fire is terror, in the cloud the gentle allurement of vision. Day is the life of the just; night, of the sinner. Hence Eph. 5: You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord, etc. By day the pillar was shown through a cloud, and by night through fire; because almighty God will appear both gentle to the just and terrible to the impious. Coming to judgment, he soothes the former by the mildness of gentleness, and terrifies the latter by the strictness of justice. Otherwise: the pillar of cloud went before the people in the wilderness, and shone with the splendor of fire not by day but by night: because Christ, giving leadership to those who follow by the example of his way of life, shone with no light to those who trust in their own justice; but to those who recognize the darkness of sins he shone with the fire of his love. Christ is cloud and pillar, because upright and firm and supporting our weakness; because shining by night, not shining by day, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John 9). The sacrament of Christ also is manifest as by day in the flesh, as in a cloud: but in judgment as in a nocturnal terror; because then there will be great tribulation, it will shine like fire to the just, and burn the unjust.
14.2: 14.2 Pihahiroth, which is between Migdol, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 5 on Exodus. Let us see what road is commanded to be chosen. From Etham, he says, turn back and make your way between Epauleum and Migdol, which is opposite Baal-zephon, etc. Epauleum is a winding ascent, Migdol a tower, Baal-zephon is interpreted ascent of a watchtower, or having a watchtower. Perhaps he thought God would show a level and easy road, but it is an ascent and a winding one. For the way by which one strives toward the virtues is not downhill, but is climbed narrowly and with difficulty. Hence Matt. 7: Narrow and strait is the way that leads to life. The road, then, on which one advances is a winding ascent, and an ascent of a watchtower or having a watchtower. The ascent pertains to deeds, the watchtower to faith; it is shown therefore that both in deeds and in faith there is much difficulty, much labor: for many temptations meet us, many stumbling blocks, as we wish to do the things that are God's. Then in faith you will find many winding things, very many questions, objections of heretics, contradictions of unbelievers: this road, then, is to be traveled by those who follow the Lord. But there is also a tower on this road, of which it is said, Luke 14: Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to finish it? This tower, then, is steep and lofty from these virtues; seeing which Pharaoh says: These men are wandering. With Pharaoh, whoever follows God is said to wander, because the way of wisdom is winding, having many difficulties and turnings. If you confess one invisible Father, and his one only-begotten Jesus Christ, and one Holy Spirit, this seems winding, difficult and incredible among unbelievers. If you say that the God of majesty is crucified, the son of man who came down from heaven: these things seem winding and difficult; whoever hears them, unless he hears with faith, says that these men are wandering. But you be fixed in this faith, knowing that God shows you this way of faith, who says: Taking your camp from Etham, pitch it between Epauleum and Migdol. It would have been. ORIGEN. Fleeing Egypt you come to the ascent of work and faith, and to the building of the tower: you come to the sea, and the waves of temptations meet you. Hence 2 Tim. 3: All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, because our life upon earth is a temptation. But if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, Egypt pursues you. But see what will happen: The angel of the Lord, he says, who went before the camp of Israel, removed and went behind them. And the pillar of cloud also removed from before their face and stood behind them, and came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel. This pillar of cloud is made a wall for the people of God: upon the Egyptians it lays darkness; the pillar of fire is not transferred to the Egyptians to let them see light: but that of cloud, that they may remain in darkness, because they loved darkness, not light. And you, therefore, if you depart from the Egyptians, if you flee from the power of demons, see how many helps are prepared for you, provided you remain strong in faith: let neither the cavalry and chariots of the Egyptians terrify you, nor cry out against the law of God, that is Moses, saying: As though there were no graves in Egypt, you have brought us out.
14.11: 14.11 Perhaps there were no graves, etc.? ORIGEN, Hom. 5 on Exodus. These are the words of a mind failing in temptation: blessed is he who so receives temptations that no thought of doubt creeps upon him. To Peter also it is said, Matt. 13 [sic]: O you of little faith, why did you doubt? These are words of temptation and frailty. Otherwise it is false, for it is better to die in the wilderness than to serve the Egyptians. For he who dies in the wilderness, by this very fact that he is separated from the Egyptians, that is, from the rulers of darkness and from the power of Satan, has had some progress, even if he could not arrive at full perfection. For it is better to die on the way for one seeking the perfect life than not to set out at all. Hence the opinion of those seems mistaken who, when they set out the steep and dangerous road of virtue, judge that it should not even be begun. For it is better to die on the journey than to be slain among the Egyptians and overwhelmed by false and bitter waves.
14.13: 14.13 For the Egyptians whom you now see, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 5 [sic] on Exodus. For as you have seen the Egyptians today, you shall see them no more forever. How are these words to be taken, since the Israelites afterwards saw the Egyptians? Is it because those who then saw them did not see them again, since both those who pursued died, and these all died, each on the day of his death? For their descendants saw the descendants of those. Or, you shall not see them as today, is to be understood: not as today, pursuing and hostile, so that there is no question even about the eternal time which he put here, since even if both will see each other at the time of the resurrection, it will not be as today.
14.15: 14.15 Why do you cry to me? etc. GREGORY. Our words do not make voices in the ears of God, but our desires. For if we ask eternal life with the mouth and do not desire it with the heart, crying out we are silent: but if we desire with the heart, and are silent with the mouth, being silent we cry out. Hence in the wilderness, when the people were clamoring with voices, and Moses was silent from the din of words, he is heard in silence, and it is said to him: Why do you cry to me? For in desire a secret cry does not reach human ears, but fills the divine. ORIGEN, as above. No voice of Moses is heard, and the Lord says: Why do you cry to me? I would like to know how the saints cry to God without voice. The Apostle says to the Galatians, ch. 4: Because God will give the Spirit of his Son in our hearts, crying: Abba, Father. And he adds: The Spirit himself intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings. And again, Rom. 8: He who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires. So, then, as the Holy Spirit petitions, the cry of the saints is heard in silence. Moses is commanded to strike the sea with the rod, that it may yield to the entering people of God, and the waters which were feared, made a wall on the right and the left, not only know no destruction but even offer protection. The liquid takes on solidity, and the floor of the sea dries to dust: understand the goodness of the Creator, if you obey his will, if you follow his law, he compels the elements to serve you against their nature. I have heard it handed down from the elders that for each tribe a separate division of the waters was made, and a proper way for each. And this is shown by what is said in Psalm 135: Who divided the Red Sea into parts, etc. And elsewhere, Psalm 67: There is Benjamin the youngest in ecstasy, the princes of Judah, their rulers, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali: a proper entrance seems to be enumerated for each tribe. The Apostle says that baptism was consummated in Moses in the cloud and in the sea, so that you who are baptized in Christ, in water and in the Spirit, may know that you are pursuing the Egyptians and calling them back to servitude, namely the rulers of the world and the spiritual wickednesses whom you formerly served. But you go down into the water, and come out unharmed, and ascend new, washed from the filth of sins, ready to sing a new song. The Egyptians pursuing are drowned in the abyss, and they seem to beg Jesus not to drown them again in the abyss. THE SAME. Otherwise, if you flee Egypt, that is, the darkness of ignorance, if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, and the sea meets you, that is, the waves of those who contradict, strike with the rod also the struggling waters, that is, with the word of the law and the vigilance of the Scriptures; open a road for yourself by disputing through your adversaries, and the waves will yield to the victor, and, with those who before contradicted marveling and fixed in amazement, you will cut the straight way of faith by the lawful lines of disputations, and you will advance so far by the word of doctrine that your hearers, whom you have instructed in the words of the law, now rise up against the Egyptians like the waves of the sea, and not only assail them but overcome and destroy them. For he destroys Egypt who does not do the works of darkness, who lives not carnally but spiritually; who either expels filthy thoughts from the heart or does not receive them at all, according to Eph. 6: Taking the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one. In this way, then, we too can see the Egyptians dead today, and Pharaoh himself, if we live with such faith that God quickly crushes Satan under our feet through Jesus Christ.
14.19: 14.19 And the angel of God, removing, etc. STRABO. The angel, which is interpreted messenger, signifies the teachers, who announce to us the precepts of life, and with the cloud, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, go before the camp of Israel, that is, the Church, because they preside with knowledge of the Scriptures. When the Egyptians come upon them he goes behind, because in the time of persecution they will set themselves against it for those subject to them. The cloud was dark to the Egyptians, bright to the Hebrews.
14.21: 14.21 All that night, etc. Because during all the time of this life, which the night signifies, the grace of the Holy Spirit makes the waters of baptism passable to the faithful, that they may pass from spiritual Egypt into the promised land: but it suffocates the army of the enemies. ISIDORE. The Red Sea signifies baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ; the enemies following behind with the king die, because past sins are destroyed in baptism, and the devil is suffocated: the Egyptians press on as far as the sea, and sins as far as baptism. After the crossing of the Red Sea the people sing, the unbelieving enemies being drowned; and the faithful, ascending from the washing, their sins extinguished, sing a hymn, saying: Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously, etc.
15.1: 15.1 Then Moses sang, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 6 on Exodus. We read many songs in the Scriptures, but this is the first of all, which is sung after the victory, the Egyptians and Pharaoh being drowned. It is the custom of the saints, when the adversary is conquered, because they know that the victory was won not by their own strength but by the grace of God, to offer God a hymn of glorification. Those who sing take timbrels in their hands, as is related of Miriam and Aaron [sic]. And you too, if you have crossed the Red Sea, if you have seen the Egyptians drowned and Pharaoh cast into the abyss, can sing a hymn to God with thanksgiving, and say: Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously, etc. You will say this more worthily if you have a timbrel in your hand, that is, if you have crucified your flesh with its vices and concupiscences. For gloriously, etc. ORIGEN. It is not enough, he has been glorified; for it is one thing to be glorified, another to be gloriously glorified. When Christ took flesh for us, he was glorified, he who came to seek what had perished, yet not gloriously, because he had no form or comeliness; he was glorified when he came to the cross and endured death; hence John 17: Father, the hour is come, glorify your Son, etc. The passion of the cross was therefore also glory, where he was glorified, not gloriously indeed, but humbly; hence Phil. 2: He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. And Wisdom 2: Let us condemn him to a most shameful death. In these things, then, he was glorified humbly of himself, not gloriously; hence Luke 24: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glory? When he shall come in the glory of the Father and of the angels to judge the earth, and shall slay the true Pharaoh, that is the devil, with the spirit of his mouth, when he shall shine forth in the majesty of the Father: then he will be gloriously glorified, when all shall honor the Son as they honor the Father. He is magnified; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea, etc. In the signs of Egypt. But he was gloriously magnified, because he drowned Pharaoh and his army. Or he was magnified by working miracles before the passion, by preaching, by dying on the cross: but he was gloriously magnified when he rose again as victor, the devil conquered and hell despoiled. The horse, etc. ORIGEN. The men who pursue us are horses; and all who are born in the flesh are figuratively horses, and have their riders. There are some whom the Lord rides, and they go around the whole earth; of whom it is said, Hab. 3: Your horsemanship is salvation. Others the devil and his angels ride. Judas was a horse, and when he had the Lord as rider, he was of the horsemanship of salvation: for with the other apostles he was sent and gave salvation to the sick and healing to the languishing; but when he subjected himself to the devil, who entered into him after the morsel, being made Satan's horse and led by his reins, he rode against the Lord. All persecutors, then, are neighing horses, but they have evil angels, by whom as riders they are driven, and therefore they are fierce. If you see your persecutor raging excessively, know that he is spurred by the rider, and therefore is savage and truculent.
15.2: 15.2 He is my God, etc. ORIGEN. He will be both my God and the God of my father. Our Father who made and begot us is Christ, who said, John 16: I go to my Father, etc. If therefore I acknowledge that he is my God, I will glorify him; if also that he is the God of my father, I will exalt him: for the understanding is deeper how Christ, to bind together and unite the truth of one God, calls God his own him whom by nature he knows as Father.
15.3: 15.3 The Lord is as a man of war, etc. ORIGEN. Another reading: The Lord will crush wars. Amos 9: The Lord is his name. He crushes not only visible battles, but also those which are against us from the principalities and powers and rulers of this darkness.
15.5: 15.5 They went down into the depth like a stone. ORIGEN. Because such were not the stones from which children of Abraham would be raised up, but loved the deep and liquid element, that is, the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things. Hence of them it is said: They sank like lead in the mighty water. Sinners are heavy, and iniquity is read to sit upon a talent of lead: hence the wicked are sunk into the deep like lead, but the saints walk upon the waters, because they are light and not weighed down by the weight of sin. Christ walked upon the waters, who truly did no sin: Peter also walked, but doubted a little; for he had something of lead, on account of which it is said to him, Matt. 14: O you of little faith, why did you doubt? All are saved through fire, so that if perchance anything of the nature of lead has been admitted, the fire may boil it off and dissolve it, that all may be made the best gold, for the gold of that land which the saints are to have is the best; and as the furnace tries gold, so tribulation tries just men. All must therefore come to the furnace. For God sits and refines, and purifies the sons of Judah. If someone has brought many good works and little iniquity, that little is dissolved and purged as by fire, and the whole remains pure gold. If someone has brought more lead, he is more burned, that he may be more thoroughly refined; so that even if little, still some purified gold remains; but he who comes wholly leaden is sunk like lead in the mighty water.
15.7: 15.7 You sent forth your wrath, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 55 on Exodus. Another reading: You sent forth your spirit, and the sea covered them, etc. Behold, now for the fifth time the Spirit of God is mentioned, etc., down to Scripture merely commanding without the help of grace.
15.11: 15.11 Who is like you, etc. ORIGEN, as above. He does not compare God to the idols of the nations, nor to the demons who falsely claim for themselves the name of gods, but says that those are gods who are called so through grace and participation in God, according to Psalm 81: I have said: You are gods. And ibid.: God stood in the congregation of gods. But although these are capable of God, and seem to be granted this name through grace, none is like him in power or nature; what is said, we shall be like him, this likeness is referred not to nature but to grace, as a picture is like the one whose image is expressed in it, as to grace, but far unlike as to substance. For that is the appearance of flesh and the beauty of a living body; this is a dye of colors, and wax laid on tablets lacking sense. Among the gods, therefore, none is like the Lord, who is invisible, incorporeal, unchangeable, without beginning and without end. None is creator of all but the Father creating all things through the Son, and sanctifying all things in the Holy Spirit.
15.12: 15.12 You stretched out, etc. ORIGEN. It warns me that he says: You stretched out your right hand and the earth swallowed them, as though the cause of their being swallowed by the earth were that he stretched out his right hand. If you consider how the Lord, lifted up on the cross, stretched out his hand all day to an unbelieving and contradicting people, and how the death of iniquity oppressed the unfaithful people who cried: Crucify, crucify him (John 19), you will find how he stretched out his right hand, and the earth swallowed them. Yet there is no need to despair altogether. For if one who has been swallowed comes to his senses, he can be vomited forth like Jonah. All of us were at some time swallowed by the earth and held in the inner parts of hell: therefore Christ descended not only to the earth but also to the lower parts of the earth: and there he found us swallowed and sitting in the shadow of death; leading us out thence not only of the earth, lest we be swallowed again, he prepares the kingdom of heavens. ORIGEN. Even today the earth swallows the impious, who always think of the earth, do earthly things, speak of the earth, litigate, desire earth, place their hope in it, do not look to heaven, do not think of the future, do not fear the judgment of God nor desire his promises; when you see such a one, say that the earth has swallowed him: and if you see anyone given to luxury and the pleasures of the body, in whom the mind avails nothing but lust possesses the whole, say that the earth has swallowed him.
15.14: 15.14 They went up, etc. ORIGEN. The nations heard and were angry, sorrows took hold of the inhabitants of Philistia, etc. As to the history, it is agreed that none of these nations was present at the wonders: how then were the Philistines and Moabites and Edom, and the other nations he enumerates, terrified by fear or angered? But spiritually you will find that the Philistines, that is, those falling by the cup, and Edom, that is, earthly, tremble: and their princes run about and fear, gripped by pains, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, penetrated by him who descended into the lower parts of the earth to rescue those possessed by death. Hence they fear and tremble, for they have felt the greatness of his arm; hence also the inhabitants of Canaan, that is, the changeable and mobile, melted away, when they saw their kingdoms moved and the strong man bound. Let fear and trembling come upon them: the demons tremble and fear the cross of Christ, on which they were triumphed over, and stripped of their principalities and power. Fear and trembling, then, will fall upon them, when they see in us the sign of the cross faithfully fixed, and the greatness of the arm which the Lord spread out on the cross, as Isaiah 65 says: All the day I have spread out my hands to an unbelieving people, etc. They will not fear you otherwise, nor will your trembling fall upon them, unless they see in you the cross of Christ, so that you may say: But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 6).
15.15: 15.15 Let them become immovable as a stone, etc. ORIGEN. To become like a stone is not to be a stone by nature. For it would not become unless what it was not. We have said this on account of those who say that Pharaoh or the Egyptians were of an evil nature, and were not brought to this by freedom of choice; and who accuse God the Creator as cruel, as though he turned men into stones: he did not say, Let them become as stones, and stop, but fixed a time and measure of dominion, namely until your people pass over. The former people who were before us became like a hard and unbelieving stone, not that the nature of a stone should remain, but until the people which the Lord has acquired pass over. Hence Rom. 11: Blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and then all Israel should be saved; which through unbelief was made like a stone, hence Matt. 3: God is able of these stones to raise up children to Abraham. But since he is the creator of all, how is he said to have acquired what is not doubtful to be his? For it is said in the canticle of Deuteronomy: Is not he himself the Lord your God, who made and created you, and acquired you? (Deut. 32). For each seems to acquire what was not his. Hence heretics say of the Savior that those whom he acquired were not his: for having paid a price he bought men whom the Creator had made, and they say it is certain that each buys what is not his. For the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 7: You are bought with a price. But hear the Prophet: You were sold for your sins, and for your iniquities I put away your mother (Isa. 50). We are all, then, creatures of God, but each is sold by his sins and departs from the Creator. We are God's, then, insofar as we were created by him: but made servants of the devil insofar as we were sold by our sins. But Christ, coming, redeemed us who served the devil, to whom we sold ourselves by sinning, and so he seems to have received his own, whom he created; and to have acquired the alien, who by sinning had acquired a foreign lord. But rightly he is said to have redeemed us, who gave his blood as the price for us. But what did the devil give such that he bought us? Murder is the devil's money, for he was a murderer from the beginning: you committed murder, you received the devil's money. The same must be said of adultery, sacrilege, theft, false witness and the like: with this money he buys and makes his servants all who have taken any amount from such wealth of his.
15.17: 15.17 You shall bring them in and plant them, etc. ORIGEN. The Lord does not wish us to plant in Egypt, nor in low and humble places, but on the mountain of his inheritance. Of this planting the Prophet says, Psalm 79: You have brought a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations and planted it: you were the guide of the way in its sight, and you planted its roots, and it filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow, and its branches were the cedars of God. Do you see how and where God plants? He does not plant in valleys, but on mountains, in lofty and sublime places. For those whom he leads out of Egypt, that is the world, to faith, he does not wish to place again in lowly places, but that their way of life be sublime, and that they dwell on mountains and in high places, not creep along the earth. He no longer wishes his vine to have its fruits cast down in a lowly place, but its shoots to be led upward, placed on high, made into trailing vines: and trailing vines not on lowly trees, but on the lofty and highest cedars of God, namely the prophets and apostles: if we are joined to them, the vine which God transferred from Egypt, and our shoots are spread through their branches, and, interwoven with them, we are made trailing vines bound by the bonds of charity to one another, we shall bear very much fruit. For every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. 3). In your most firm dwelling, etc. ORIGEN. In the prepared dwelling which you have prepared, O Lord. See the goodness of the merciful Lord: he does not wish to lead you into labor, he does not wish you to make a dwelling for yourself; he will lead you into a dwelling already prepared. Hence John 4: Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors. Your sanctuary, etc. ORIGEN. Your holy place, O Lord, etc. The tabernacle of God, or the temple, is called a holy place because it sanctifies those who approach. Hebrews 9: this is not said to be made by the hand of men, but by the hand of God: for your sake, therefore, God both plants and builds; he is made farmer and builder, so that nothing may be lacking to you. Hence the Apostle, 1 Cor. 3: You are God's husbandry, God's building. What then is this holy place prepared not by the hand of men, but of God? Proverbs 9: Wisdom has built herself a house, that is, the flesh of Christ, not by the hand of man, that is, not by human work: the temple of the flesh is built in the Virgin, but the stone cut without hands grew and became a great mountain (Dan. 2): this is the holy place of the assumed flesh, cut without hands and without the work of men from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh.
15.18: 15.18 The Lord shall reign, etc. ORIGEN. O Lord, who reign forever and ever and yet. Whenever it is said forever, a length of time is indicated, but that there is some end; and if forever and ever is said, something longer is indicated, yet an end is set: and whenever ages of ages are named, perhaps, though unknown to us, some limit fixed by God is indicated. But what is added here, and yet, leaves no sense of any limit or end: for whatever you think of in which you suppose the end to stand, the prophetic word always says to you, and yet; as if it said to you, You think the Lord will reign forever and ever, and yet you think for ages of ages: and yet, and whatever you say about the spans of his kingdom, the prophet always says to you, and yet.
15.19: 15.19 But the children of Israel, etc. ORIGEN. You too, if you are a son of Israel, can walk on dry ground in the midst of the sea. If you are in the midst of a wicked and perverse nation, walking like the light of the sun in the midst of sinners, the moisture of sin will not soak you, and as you pass through this world no wave of lust will sprinkle you, no heat of covetousness will beat you. He who is Egypt, and follows Pharaoh, is sunk in the waves of vices. But he who follows Christ, and walks as he walked, has the water made a wall to him on the right and on the left. He himself walks in the middle of the way, on dry ground does not turn to the right or to the left, until he goes out to freedom and sings the hymn of victory to the Lord, saying: Let us sing to the Lord, etc.
15.20: 15.20 The timbrel. STRABO. According to Jerome it is a kind of trumpet having at the top a reed or pipe, through which it gives out a sonorous sound. The chorus, according to the same, is a simple skin with two pipes; through one it is blown, through the other it gives the sound: through both, therefore, the narrow understanding of the old law is designated. How short and small it is is shown by the fact that it is carried by a woman's hand. According to Cassiodorus the timbrel is a skin stretched between two pieces of wood: by which the maceration of the flesh is designated. The chorus is a multitude singing together and is called chorus as if the song of contemporaries. Because in a chorus all voices resound equally, charity is signified by it, by which we are all one in Christ. Whoever therefore renders praises to God in jubilation, let him do this in the chorus, that is in charity, and in the timbrel, that is in the mortification of the flesh. Hence Psalm 150: Praise him with timbrel and chorus, etc.
15.22: 15.22 And Moses brought Israel, etc. The baptized are led through the world as through a desert after the crossing of the Red Sea, not yet having the promised country, but hoping and waiting through patience, while they are wearied by laborious and dangerous temptation. But lest they return in heart to Egypt, Christ does not abandon them there: for that pillar also does not withdraw.
15.23: 15.23 And they came, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 6 on Exodus. After the crossing of the Red Sea, after the choruses and timbrels, after the triumphal hymns, they come to Marah, bitter water, which the people could not drink; they come to the danger of thirst. But Moses cried to the Lord, and he showed him a tree, by which the water was made sweet, and there God gave him justices and judgment; where there was bitterness, where there was thirst, and, what is graver, in an abundance of waters, there was no other place more worthy and fit. Besides, what it says, God showed him a tree, and he cast it into the water, and it was made sweet, as though God could not make water sweet without a tree, or Moses did not know the tree. But if the law is taken according to the letter, it is bitter, and Marah itself. For what is so bitter as that a boy on the eighth day should receive the wound of circumcision, and that tender infancy should suffer the harshness of iron? Bitter is the cup of the law: the people of God, not that which was baptized in Moses in the cloud and in the sea, but that in spirit and water, cannot drink and taste it, nor bear the bitterness of the victims, nor the observance of the sabbath. But if God shows the tree to be cast into this bitterness, the water of the law becomes sweet and drinkable. Proverbs 3: Wisdom is a tree of life to all who embrace her. If therefore the tree of the wisdom of Christ is cast into the law, showing how circumcision, the sabbath, the law of leprosy and such things ought to be understood, the bitterness of the law is turned into the sweetness of spiritual understanding, so that the people which left the idols and fled to God can drink. If it hears the law teaching about sacrifices, it at once flees and cannot drink. Into this bitterness, then, that is the letter of the law, God placed justices and testimonies, as in a small vessel he encloses [placed] the treasures of his wisdom and knowledge. Hence: We have this treasure in earthen vessels (2 Cor. 3 [sic]). So that this water may be drunk, God shows a tree to be cast into it, that whoever drinks may not die, may not feel the bitterness. If anyone, therefore, drinks without the tree of life, that is, without the mystery of the cross, without the faith of Christ, without spiritual understanding, he will die of the bitterness. Hence: The letter kills, that is, the water of Marah, if it is drunk unchanged and not turned into sweetness.
15.25: 15.25 Who showed him, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 57 on Exodus. Was it a kind of wood having this power: or could God, who did such great wonders, have done it with any wood? What is said, he showed him, however, seems to signify as though it were already such; unless perhaps it was a place where no trees at all were found, so that this very thing was of divine help, that the Lord showed him a tree where there was none, and through the tree made the waters sweet, prefiguring the glory and grace of the cross. But in such a tree also who is to be praised if not the creator and the one who showed it? There he established precepts for him. ORIGEN, Hom. 7 on Exodus. Why did he add: After God gave him justices and judgments, there he tested him, saying: If you will hear the voice of the Lord your God. He seems to explain why he gave the justifications and judgments, namely to test them whether they would hear the voice of the Lord God and keep his commandments. For as to the former people, what good or perfect thing was commanded to them, murmuring and contradicting, who a little later, forgetful of the wonders of God, turn to idols? Precepts are given, therefore, in which they are tested; hence: I gave them precepts and justifications that were not good, in which they shall not live (Ezek. 20). For tested in the precepts they are not found faithful, and therefore the commandment which was unto life was found by them to be unto death. For the same commandment, if kept, begets life; if not kept, death. To those who do not keep them, therefore, the commandments are said not to be good, and ones in which they shall not live. But with the wood of the cross mixed in, turned into sweetness, and spiritually understood, the commandments of life were kept. All the sickness which I put upon Egypt, I will not bring upon you. He seems to say that if one keeps the commandments, he suffers no illness, that is, neither fevers nor other bodily pains. But Job, the most just and full of all piety, is filled from head to foot with the worst ulcer. But the just do not have those infirmities which the Egyptians have. Egypt is the world: to love the world and the things that are in the world is the Egyptian sickness; to observe months and times, to cling to the courses of the stars, to serve the flesh, to give oneself to luxury and be free for delights, is the Egyptian sickness. And they came, etc. ORIGEN, ibid. The people are not led first to Elim, where there were twelve fountains of water, in which was no bitterness, but much pleasantness from the density of palms: but first they were led to salt and bitter waters, which, sweetened by the tree shown by the Lord, they come to the fountains. If we follow the history alone, it does not much edify us to know to which place they came first, to which second. But first the people are led to the letter of the law, from which, while it remains in its bitterness, it cannot withdraw. When it has been sweetened by the tree of life and understood spiritually, it passes from the Old Testament to the New, and to the twelve apostolic fountains, where seventy palm trees are found. For not only the twelve apostles preached the faith of Christ, but also the other seventy, through whom the world recognized the palms of Christ's victory.
