It is not enough, therefore, for the people of God to drink the water of Marah, though sweetened by the tree of life; the Old Testament alone is not enough to drink, for one must come to the New, from which one drinks without scruple and difficulty. The Jews are even now at Marah, that is, at the bitter waters: for God has not yet shown them the tree by which they become sweet, because unless they believe, they will not understand (Isa. 7).
16.2: 16.2 And the whole congregation of Israel murmured, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 7 on Exodus. O ungrateful people! It longs for Egypt, though it has seen the Egyptians destroyed; and for the flesh of Egypt, though it sees the flesh of the Egyptians given to fishes and birds! It murmurs against Moses, indeed against God; but at first it is forgiven, and a second time and perhaps a third: but if they do not stop but persist, hear what follows; it is related in the book of Numbers (Num. 21), and the same Apostle repeats it, saying, 1 Cor. 10: Neither murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by serpents. These things were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. But if we do not cease to murmur and complain against God, we shall incur a like danger or example of offense. For when we complain about the unseasonableness of the weather, the unfruitfulness of crops, the scarcity of rains, and the prosperity of some and the unprosperity of others, we murmur against God. But these things are forgiven at first; for those who persist they are gravely avenged, because serpents will be sent upon them, that is, they will be handed over to unclean and poisoning spirits, who with hidden bites feed on the inner parts of the heart. ORIGEN. For the correction of readers the sin of the people is pointed out: that it murmured and was ungrateful for divine benefits, when it had received the heavenly manna. In the second month, on the fifteenth day of the month, which is not written without reason. Recall the laws of the Passover which were stated in Numbers 9, and you will find that this is the time appointed for making the second Passover for those who were unclean in soul, or occupied with business in foreign parts. Those who were not unclean in soul, or were not traveling far, made the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month; those traveling far, and the unclean, make the second Passover at this time, in which manna descended from heaven. On the day on which the first Passover is made, manna does not descend, but on that on which the second: the first Passover is that of the Jewish people; the second, ours. For we were unclean in soul, who worshipped idols; and we were foreigners and far off, guests and strangers to the covenants of God, etc. (Eph. 2). But manna is given from heaven, not on the day on which the first Passover is made, but on which the second: for the bread that came down from heaven (John 6) did not come to those who were celebrating the first solemnity, but to us who have taken up the second. For Christ our Passover is sacrificed, who, true man, is the bread come down from heaven (1 Cor. 5). Let us see meanwhile what is shown to have been done on this day: On the fourteenth day of the second month the people murmured, etc.
16.3: 16.3 We sat over the fleshpots, etc. They had flocks of sheep and herds of oxen from which they could eat; but they burned with desire for the fish and birds in which Egypt abounds.
16.4: 16.4 Behold, I will rain, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 8 on Exodus. I would like first to have a discussion on this Scripture with the Jews, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted, as to what seems to them about what is said: Six days continuously you shall gather, but on the sixth day double. It appears therefore that the sixth day is named which is placed before the sabbath; and the sabbath is the seventh day. I ask, then, on which day manna began to be given? and I wish to compare our Lord's day with the sabbath of the Jews. For from Scripture it appears that manna is first given on the Lord's day, gathered six days continuously; on the seventh, which is the sabbath, there is a rest. Because therefore God rained manna on the Lord's day, and not on the sabbath, let the Jews understand that already then our Lord's day was preferred to their sabbath; and it is indicated that on that day the grace of God did not descend to them from heaven, and the heavenly bread, which is the word of God, did not reach them; hence Hosea 3: For many days the children of Israel shall sit without king, without prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priest. But on our Lord's day the Lord always rains manna, that is, the heavenly words which are joyful to us. Those unhappy ones also sigh for manna like their fathers, and are not worthy to receive it; for they cannot eat what is small like coriander seed and white as hoarfrost. For they feel nothing in the word of God small, subtle and spiritual, but all fat and gross. For the heart of this people is made gross. The interpretation of this name also sounds the same. For manna is interpreted What is this? The very force of the name invites to learning, that when you hear the law of God recited, you may always inquire and say to the teachers, What is this? You, then, if you wish to eat manna and receive the word of God, know that it is small and very subtle, like coriander seed: for it has something of an herb with which to nourish and refresh the weak. For the weak eats herbs (Rom. 14). It has also something of hoarfrost's stiffness, and therefore is like hoarfrost; but of whiteness and sweetness very much. What is whiter, more splendid, than divine instruction? What sweeter, more pleasant than the words of God, which are above honey and the honeycomb? Loaves. Manna, namely: it is a mode of speech by which bread is put for food; and Scripture likes to say loaves in the plural rather than bread in the singular. That I may test. This testing is a trial, not a seduction to sin; nor are they tested so that God might not know: but he shows them to themselves, that they may become more humble to ask help and to recognize the grace of God.
16.5: 16.5 But on the sixth day, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 7. On the sixth day let double be gathered into storage, as much as will suffice even for the sabbath. The sixth day is this life in which we now are, hence in six days God made this world; on this day, therefore, we ought to lay up as much as will suffice for the future. For whatever good work you acquire here, whatever of justice, mercy and piety you commend, this will be food for you in the future. For he who acquires here ten talents (Luke 19) will receive there ten cities, and whatever a man sows, that also he shall reap (Gal. 6). The rich of this age store up those things which are corrupted in this age, indeed with this age: but good things stored up remain until the morrow. It is written: Those who were unfaithful kept some of the manna, and worms boiled up from it and it rotted; but what was stored for the sabbath day remained whole. And you therefore, if you lay up treasure for the sake of the present life and love of the world, worms at once boil up, of which Isaiah 66 says: Their worm shall not die; avarice and the blind desire of riches generate these in those who have money and, seeing their brothers in need, shut up their bowels against them. Hence the Apostle, 1 Tim. 6, commands the rich not to be high-minded, nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches, etc.; and worms are made in us from nowhere else than from manna, that is, the word of God. Hence John 15: If I had not come and spoken to them, etc. After the word of God is received, therefore, if anyone sins, the word itself becomes a worm, which always digs at his conscience and gnaws the hidden recesses of the breast.
16.6: 16.6 ORIGEN. In the evening you shall know, etc. In the evening you shall know that I am the Lord; and in the morning you shall see the majesty of the Lord. Let the Jews answer me how the Lord is known in the evening, and his majesty seen in the morning? Where was he known in the evening, and his majesty seen in the morning? But this is not understood except in the Gospel (Matt. 28), in which in the evening of the sabbath, which dawns into the first of the sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to the sepulcher, and found the stone rolled back from the tomb, an earthquake made, and the tombs open, and the centurion and the guards of the sepulcher saying: Truly this was the Son of God. The Lord was known in this evening, because he was the Lord: he was known in the power of the resurrection, and in the morning his glory was seen. When the other women came on the first of the sabbath very early, they found angels with great brightness sitting at the sepulcher, and saying: He is not here, but is risen from the dead. Come and see the place, etc. (Luke 24). His majesty was seen, therefore, in the morning, because the resurrection was also announced through angels.
16.7: 16.7 And what are we, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 59 on Exodus, vol. 3. They wished that he not avail as much as God, etc., down to he showed the Holy Spirit to be God by adding, Acts 5: You have not lied to men, but to God.
16.12: 16.12 In the evening you shall eat flesh. ORIGEN, as above. Morally we can understand that for each of us the morning is the beginning of the day, the time when we are first enlightened and kindled to the light of faith. In this time we cannot eat the flesh of the word, that is, we are not yet capable of perfect doctrine; but after long exercises, after much progress, when we are now near to the evening, that is, the faith of perfection, then we are made capable of more solid food. Let us hasten therefore to receive manna, which gives a taste in the mouth as each one wishes. Hence Matt. 9: Be it done to you according to your faith. And you therefore, if you receive the word of God that is preached in the Church with all faith and devotion, let whatever you desire be done to you. If you are afflicted, it consoles you, saying: A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise (Ps. 50); if you rejoice for the hope of the future, it heaps joys upon you, saying: Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you just (Ps. 31); if you are irascible, it says: Cease from anger, and forsake wrath (Ps. 36); if you are in pains, it heals you, saying: The Lord heals all your diseases (Matt. 4 [sic]); if you are consumed by poverty, it says in consolation: The Lord lifts the needy from the earth, and raises the poor from the dunghill (Ps. 112). If anyone, however, receives it unfaithfully, and does not eat but hides it, worms boil up from it. Nor be troubled if the word of God is brought to this, that it is thought to become a worm; for he himself says: I am a worm and no man (Ps. 21). For as he is the one who is made a ruin to some, and to others a resurrection (Luke 2); so also he is the one who in manna is made the sweetness of honey to the faithful, a worm to the unfaithful. For he is the word of God who rebukes the minds of the wicked and pierces the conscience with the darts of corrections. He is also the one who is made fire for those to whom he opens the Scriptures, who say: Was not our heart burning within us? etc. (Luke 24). To others he is fire, with which he burns the thorns from the bad earth, that is, consumes evil thoughts in the heart; and therefore for sinners neither does the rebuking worm ever die, nor is the burning fire extinguished: but to the just and faithful it remains sweet and pleasant. Hence it is said in Psalm 33: Taste and see, etc. ORIGEN, as above. Another reading: In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with loaves. Let the Jews say what is the logic, that in the evening they eat flesh without loaves, or in the morning loaves without relish? What of the divine gift, what of the tempering of heavenly grace is shown in this? Is this what lets them recognize God, who eat flesh in the evening without loaves, and say that the majesty of God appears if again loaves are eaten without flesh? Let them keep these things for those who, agreeing with you, think that God is recognized in quails; but we, to whom at the end, at the evening of the world, the Word was made flesh, say that God is recognized only in that flesh which he took from the Virgin: for this flesh of the Word of God no one has eaten either in the morning or at noon, but in the evening: for the coming of the Lord in the flesh was made toward evening, as John also says: Little children, it is the last hour (1 John 2).
16.14: 16.14 Like hoarfrost upon the ground. Hoarfrost signifies Christ: for manna was first given on the Lord's day, and Christ rose on the Lord's day. Pounded. That is, most pure. For as wheat or millet or the like is ground in a small mortar with a pestle and stripped of its husks, so the body of Christ through the tribulation of the passion and the pestle of the cross was stripped of mortality. Or the small manna is the subtlety of heavenly doctrine, which is pounded with a pestle that the literal sense be stripped off.
16.15: 16.15 Manhu. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 27, ch. 7. What is signified by the manna given to the children of Israel from above, if not wonder at heavenly sweetness? For the food that is received from above is sweet; it is called man hu, which is interpreted What is this? which we say when we see what we wonder at without knowing. The soul, then, receives heavenly manna when, lifted up by the voice of compunction, it is amazed at the new appearance of eternal refreshment, so that, filled with divine sweetness, it rightly answers What is this? because while it is raised up from the lowest thought, it beholds and unwontedly wonders at the things that are from above. And when by this voice the deafness of our sluggishness is broken, the habit of the old life is changed, so that the soul, inspired by the heavenly Spirit, seeks in the highest what it had despised, and despises in the lowest what it had sought.
16.16: 16.16 According to the number of your souls, etc. AUGUSTINE, Expression 78. Scripture often calls men souls, the whole from the part: but not easily flesh for men, but flesh in the singular; as Psalm 55: I will not fear what flesh can do to me; which he says more plainly in the same psalm, what man can do to me. But it would not say, according to the number of your fleshes, as it said, according to the number of your souls.
16.18: 16.18 According to what they could eat, etc. Because in the present life everyone ought to learn as much as he can, lest he leave anything unexamined, lest when he can no longer, he begin to learn.
16.20: 16.20 But some of them left of it until the morning, etc. The beginning of the other life, in which there will be no leisure for doctrine, but the manna will rot and swarm with worms, that is, will generate eternal punishment for them.
16.21: 16.21 And when the sun grew hot, it melted. Because then the understanding of all Scripture will be open, for now we see through a glass in a dark manner, but then face to face (1 Cor. 13).
16.22: 16.22 Double food. Things necessary for soul and body, that is. For in the seventh, which is understood as the age of the dead, there will be no place for working.
16.23: 16.23 The rest of the sabbath, etc. By hearing the word of God and doing it, or by living well and showing mercy to others. What was stored for the sabbath was not corrupted, because good things done for the future rest remain whole in the future life. Otherwise worms boiled up and what was kept rotted: for those who lay up treasure for the sake of the present life and love of the world, the worm that shall not die boils up.
16.33: 16.33 And lay it up before, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 61 on Exodus. It can be asked where Aaron would lay it up before the Lord, when there was no tabernacle, nor had the ark of the testimony yet been constructed. Did he perhaps say lay up with a view to the future, so that it be understood that it could then be laid up before the Lord, when the ark was to be? Or rather was before the Lord said of what is done by the very devotion of offering, in whatever place it might be set? For where is God not? But what it adds: And Aaron laid it up before the tabernacle to be kept, asserts the former sense more. For in this way Scripture spoke by anticipation what was done afterwards when the tabernacle of the testimony began to be.
16.35: 16.35 And the children of Israel ate manna forty years, etc. AUGUSTINE, ibid., Question 62. Another reading: And the children of Israel ate manna forty years, etc., down to for God knew what they desired and with what kind of flesh to satisfy them. They ate manna forty years. The body of Christ, namely the Word of God, which we now receive in a dark manner, but then face to face (1 Cor. 13). Until they came to an inhabited land, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 63 on Exodus, vol. 3. Another reading: Until they came to the region of Phoenicia. By repetition he explains what land he said was inhabited, etc., down to for antiquity changed the names of many lands, places, rivers and cities for certain reasons.
17.1: 17.1 Then all the multitude of the children of Israel setting forth, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 11 on Exodus. All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, are assailed by enemies: and he who travels the road of this life must always be ready and stand in camp. Hence the whole synagogue of the children of Israel set out from the desert of Sin according to their camps, by the word of God. There is indeed one Synagogue of the Lord, but it is divided into four camps, which are described in Numbers around the tabernacle of the Lord on all sides. Armed, therefore, serving in the camp of the Lord, do not entangle yourself in secular business, and keep watch always in the camp of the Lord, so that it may be said of you that you set out by the word of the Lord from the desert of Sin, and came to Rephidim. Sin is interpreted temptation; Rephidim, soundness of judgment: he who comes well out of temptation comes to soundness of judgment. For on the day of judgment he will be sound. Hence Apoc. 2: To him that overcomes I will give of the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God. He comes, then, to soundness of judgment who well orders his words in judgment. Sin. Here Sin is specially taken as one station of those five that were from the Red Sea to Mount Sinai, which Josephus describes by name. Generally, indeed, all that desert is called Sin, as also Rephidim. They encamped in Rephidim. JEROME, On Hebrew Places, vol. 3. It is a place in the desert near Mount Horeb. It should be known that every wilderness as far as Mount Sinai is called Sin, and from the whole province even the place of one station took the name, as also Moab is the name both of a city and of a province. In this solitude there are five stations, Zuph, and the desert of Sin, Alush, Dophkah, Rephidim. Hence it is well said that all the multitude of the children of Israel set out from the desert of Sin by their stations according to the mouth of the Lord, and came to Rephidim. Whence it is clear that several stations are shown by the name of one region.
17.3: 17.3 And the people thirsted there, etc. ORIGEN, as above. Another reading: The people thirsted, it says, for water, and murmured against Moses. It would have sufficed to say that it thirsted; what need was there to add for water? The addition is not superfluous. There are different thirsts, and each has its own. Those who are good hunger and thirst after justice (Matt. 5). Others also say: My soul has thirsted for you, O God (Ps. 41). But sinners suffer not a thirst for water, not a hunger for bread, but for hearing the word of God. The people therefore thirsted for water, who ought to have thirsted for justice. But God, the instructor of infants, the teacher of the foolish, corrects faults and amends errors, saying to Moses to take the rod, and strike the rock, and bring forth waters. For he wishes them now to drink from the rock and to advance and to come to the inner mysteries. They murmured against Moses, therefore the Lord commands him to show them the rock from which they may drink. For if there is anyone who, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the law according to the letter displeases him because in many things it does not seem to have consistency, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst. But this rock does not give waters unless struck, and when struck it brings forth fountains: for Christ struck and slain on the cross brought forth the fountains of the New Testament. Hence Zech. 8 [sic]: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered. For unless he had been struck, and blood and water had come out of his side, we should all suffer thirst for the word of God. Hence: They drank of the spiritual rock that followed them: and the rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10). ISIDORE. The thirsting people murmured for water against Moses: therefore God commands him to show them a rock from which they may drink. If anyone, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the letter of the law displeases him, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it, that he may drink and refresh his thirst.
17.5: 17.5 Go before the people, etc. Not only does Moses lead the people to the waters, but also the elders of the people. For not the law alone announces Christ, but also the prophets and patriarchs and all the elders. And your rod, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 64 on Exodus. It is read that Aaron, not Moses, struck the river with the rod. For Moses with the same rod divided the sea, not the river. What then does it mean: Take the rod with which you struck the river? Or did he perhaps call the sea a river? and an example of this expression must be sought. Or is what Aaron did rather attributed to Moses, because God commanded through Moses what Aaron should do, and in this there is authority, in that ministry? Hence: He shall be to you for the people, and you to him in the things that pertain to God.
17.6: 17.6 And you shall strike the rock. Christ, who on the cross was struck by the Jews: to which the rod was added, that is, the wood of the passion, so that water might remain for the faithful.
17.8: 17.8 And Amalek came, etc. STRABO. Amalek was a son of Ishmael, from whom the Amalekites, who are also the Ishmaelites: these are the Saracens. It is interpreted drinking or licking blood, and signifies the devil, who always attacks the saints going out of Egypt and tending to the promised land, and desires to drink the blood of souls. ORIGEN, Hom. 11 on Exodus. The war made with the Amalekites is described. Before the people ate bread from heaven and drank water from the rock, they are not said to have fought; but it is said to them: The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace. There is, then, a time when the Lord fights for us, and does not permit us to be tempted above that which we are able, nor allow us to come, unequal in strength, to a strong encounter. Job too, already perfect, fulfilled the contest of his temptation; and you therefore, when you have begun to eat manna, the heavenly bread of the word of God, and to drink water from the rock, and have approached the inner parts of spiritual doctrine, expect the fight, prepare yourself for war.
17.9: 17.9 And Moses said to Joshua, etc. ORIGEN, ibid. Another reading: Moses said to Jesus: Choose men for yourself, etc. Up to this point there has never been mention of the blessed name of Jesus. Here for the first time Moses called Jesus, and said to him: Choose men for yourself. Moses calls Jesus, the law invokes Christ, to choose for himself mighty men from the people: Moses could not choose, but Jesus alone, who says, John 15: You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you (Matt. 12 [sic]). He is the leader of the elect and prince of the mighty. He himself fights with Amalek. For he enters the house of the strong man, and binds the strong man, and plunders his goods. I will stand on the top of the hill. ORIGEN, as above. Moses went up, it says, not to the top of the mountain, but to the top of the hill. For it was reserved to him then to go up to the top of the mountain when Jesus was to go up, and with him Moses and Elijah, and there be transfigured in glory. Now therefore, as not yet glorified by the transfiguration of Jesus, he does not go up to the top of the mountain, but to the top of the hill. And when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel overcame. Moses lifts up his hands, he does not stretch them out; Jesus, who embraced the whole world, lifted up on the cross, says: I have stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people (Isa. 65). To lift up the hands is to lift deeds to God, so that one does not have deeds cast down and lying on the ground, but pleasing to God and raised to heaven. He lifts up his hands who lays up treasure in heaven. For where the treasure is, there is the eye, there the hand. He lifts up his hands who says: The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice (Ps. 140). If our deeds are lifted up, Amalek is conquered: hence Isa. 35: Strengthen the feeble hands and the weak knees. If the people keeps the law, Moses lifts up his hands, and the adversary is conquered. If it does not keep the law, Amalek prevails. Since, then, our fight is against principalities and powers, the rulers of the darkness of this world, if you wish to conquer, lift up your hands, that is, your deeds; let your conversation not be on earth, but in heaven. You too lift up your hands to heaven, to God, fulfill the command of the Apostle: Pray without ceasing (1 Thess. 5); and then what is written will happen, that as the calf licks up the green grass in the fields, so this people will lick up the people that is upon the earth; where it is introduced that the people of God fought not so much with hand and arms as with voice and tongue, and laid low the enemies by prayer. Lift up therefore your deeds, press on in prayer: this is the fight of the Christian, which overcomes the enemy. I think, moreover, that by this figure two peoples are signified, of whom one, from the Gentiles, lifts up the hands of Moses, and raises on high what he wrote and the understanding of it, that it may thus conquer; but the other, that is the Jewish people, does not lift the hands of Moses from the earth, nor understands anything high or sublime in him, and so is conquered by its adversaries. Having the rod of God, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 65. Now it is called the rod of God, which was first called Aaron's, afterwards Moses'. As the spirit of Elijah is spoken of, which is the Spirit of God, of which Elijah is said to be a partaker; and the justice of God, which is ours. Hence: Ignorant of the justice of God, and seeking to establish their own (Rom. 10), that is, as prepared by themselves for themselves.
17.11: 17.11 And when Moses lifted up his hands, etc. STRABO. Because when the law is understood mystically, the passion of Christ is spiritually weighed, the devil is conquered and put to flight. But when the hands are let down, that is, the precepts of the law are practiced less zealously, the enemy pursues as victor.
17.12: 17.12 And taking a stone, etc. GREGORY, Hom. 33 on the Gospels. Moses sat on a stone, etc., down to those whom it justly condemns, he himself mercifully frees.
17.14: 17.14 For I will destroy, etc. RABANUS. In this he signifies that almighty God, through the law, which Moses signifies, and concerning Christ, pronounces that he will blot out the memory of the spiritual enemies. Hence Psalm 9: Their memory has perished with a noise.
17.15: 17.15 And Moses built an altar, etc. All conquerors of the devil ought to build altars of faith in their hearts, on which they may offer spiritual sacrifices.
18.1: 18.1 And when Jethro had heard, etc. That Moses, about to free the children of Israel, sent away his wife and sons, whom he afterwards received in the desert, signifies that preachers, when sent to the work of preaching, ought to unburden themselves of temporal care: but when afterwards they are taken up to the episcopate or to some other dignity, then they ought to bear solicitude for those subject to them in spiritual as well as temporal matters.
18.5: 18.5 And Jethro came, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 11 on Exodus. Another reading: After this Moses came to the mount of God, and went out of the camp to meet Jethro as he came, and did not lead him to the mount of God, but to his own tent. For the priest of Midian could not go up to the mount of God, but neither could he go down into Egypt, nor Moses' wife, but now she comes to him with her sons. For no one could go down into Egypt and undergo the contests of the Egyptians unless a proved athlete, and one who in the contest abstains from everything. Moses, because a great and powerful athlete, went down into Egypt to the contests and exercises of virtues; Abraham and Jacob also, who by that very name is an athlete, when he had gone down into Egypt, became like the stars of heaven in multitude. For others it turns out the opposite to have gone down to Egypt. I know that Jeroboam, fleeing from Solomon, went down into Egypt, and split and corrupted the people of God; because going down into Egypt he received from king Shishak as wife Tahpenes, the sister of his wife.
18.12: 18.12 So Jethro offered, etc. AUGUSTINE, in Expressions, expression 85. And Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, took burnt offerings, etc. He used took for offered: or perhaps it is the sense, not the expression, that it be understood that he took and offered them; although Moses is not read to have sacrificed, nor Aaron, nor any of the Hebrews who were brought out of the land of Egypt: yet it was said above that Moses set up an altar. But we read that Jethro was a priest of Midian, that is, of the nation of Midian. It is a wonder if at his coming Moses began to sacrifice, and not rather he himself who was the priest. And they came, etc. ORIGEN, as above. Another reading: The elders came, it says, Aaron and all Israel, to eat bread with the father-in-law of Moses in the sight of God. Not all eat bread in the sight of God, but those who are elders, who are seniors, that is, who are perfect, proved in merits, who whether they eat or drink do it to the glory of God. Everything, then, that the saints do they do in the sight of God: the sinner flees from the sight of God. Adam, after he sinned, fled from the sight of the Lord, and being asked answered: I heard your voice, Lord, and I hid myself, because I was naked (Gen. 3). Cain went out from the face of the Lord, because he was unworthy of the sight of the Lord. Therefore those who receive a fuller knowledge of God, if they do evil, do it before God. Hence Psalm 1 [sic]: Against you only have I sinned, etc. He who does evil before God at once repents and says, I have sinned. He who departs from the sight of God does not know how to be converted and to purge sin by repentance. This, then, is the difference between doing evil before God and departing from the sight of God. ORIGEN. Not in vain does Jethro come to Moses, nor in vain does he eat bread with the elders of the people in the sight of God; he gives Moses acceptable and useful counsel, that he choose men and appoint rulers of the people who worship God, are powerful and hate pride. For such ought those to be who are not proud and hate pride; that is, that not only they themselves be without vice, but that in the wicked they hate the vices: I do not say the men, but the vices. Before God, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 66. It is asked where, since there was neither a tabernacle nor the ark of the testimony, which were established afterwards? Nor can we take this as said of the future, as was said of the manna, that it was put in a vessel, a golden one. Therefore we must take it that what was done in honor of the Lord was done before God.
18.16: 18.16 I will show the precepts, etc. THE SAME, Question 67. It can be asked how Moses said here, etc., down to he could not judge justly.
18.19: 18.19 But hear my words, etc. THE SAME, Question 68. The first question is why God his servant, etc., down to by which it becomes so much the fuller as it is more freely extended to the heavenly and eternal things. Be you to the people, etc. THE SAME, Question 69. And what he adds, etc., down to but whence this can be proved I do not know.
18.21: 18.21 But provide, etc. He is instructed by a foreigner for the guarding of humility, lest he who learned so many secrets of God from God himself be puffed up and think himself not in need of human counsel. It was also prefigured that the teaching of the Gentiles would overcome the knowledge and pride of the Jews; and that the faithful from the Gentiles would suggest what was lacking in the law to be supplied, and bring spiritual understanding to the law of God. Moses also knew that the law would hear this people and do whatever it said, and that a lessening of the law would also come about at the suggestion of the Gospel. And appoint, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 11. You shall appoint them, he says, tribunes and centurions, and they shall judge the people at all times, but whatever is more weighty they shall refer to you. Let the rulers of the people and the elders of the people hear, who ought to judge the people at all times, always and without intermission sit in judgment, settle disputes, and reconcile the dissenting, call back the discordant to favor. Let each one learn his duty from the holy Scriptures. Moses, he says, is to be in the things that pertain to God, and to set forth the word of God to the people. The other rulers, whom he called tribunes because they preside over a tribe, or centurions, or commanders of fifty, preside over the lesser judgments, settling what pertains to individuals. Which figure I think is to be kept in the age to come as well. Hence Matt. 19: When the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit on twelve seats, etc. You see therefore that not only the Lord judges, to whom the Father gave all judgment (John 5), but he appoints rulers to judge lesser causes; and the word that is weightier they refer to him. Therefore the Lord says of one, Matt. 5: He shall be in danger of the council; of another, Matt. 12 [sic]: He shall be in danger of hell fire. But they are also said to give account for every idle word. And so he did not say that we shall render account to God, as of perjury. You shall perform your oaths to the Lord. Matt. 12: The queen of the south also shall rise in judgment with the men of this generation, and shall condemn it. Behold another kind of judgment, Matt. 13: He who has ears to hear, let him hear: for all these things are a shadow of heavenly things and an image of things to come. THE SAME. As it is written in Eccles. 1: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing, so we cannot be satisfied with considering what is written, with which it may edify us, in how many ways it may instruct us. For when I behold that Moses, a prophet full of God, to whom God spoke face to face (Exod. 33), received counsel from Jethro his father-in-law, priest of Midian, I am struck with exceeding admiration. For Moses heard the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he said to him. He did not say, Since God speaks to me what I ought to do, how shall I receive counsel from a man, and a gentile man, alien to the people of God? and he does not ask who says it, but listens to what is said. We therefore, if we find something wisely said by Gentiles, let us not despise the sayings along with the name of the author; nor, because we hold the law of God, is it fitting for us to swell with pride and despise the words of the prudent; but proving all things, let us hold that which is good. But those who today preside over peoples, I do not say if some things have already been revealed to them by God: but if they have any merit in knowledge of the law, disdain the counsel of an inferior, even of a priest, not to mention a layman, not to mention a gentile: but Moses, who was meek above all men (Num. 12), took the counsel of an inferior, to give to rulers a pattern of humility, and to mark the image of a future sacrament. He knew that at some time it would come about that Gentiles would offer good counsel, bringing good and spiritual understanding to the law with Moses, and the law would hear them, doing all that they said. For the law cannot do as the Jews say, because the law is weakened in the flesh, that is, in the letter, and can do nothing according to the letter. For the law brought nothing to perfection (Heb. 7). But according to this counsel which we bring to the law, all things can be done spiritually, and sacrifices offered, which cannot now be done carnally; the law of leprosy can be kept spiritually. As we therefore understand, perceive and give counsel, the law does all things: but according to the letter, not all things but few.
2.6: 2.6 And seeing the little one in it, etc. THEODORET. Mystically. Circumcision especially could have revealed this to her, for the Egyptians had not yet admitted such a mystery, although in the course of time they observed the law of circumcision in imitation of the Hebrews. Hence Jeremiah: I will consider all who circumcise the foreskin, the Egyptians and the sons of Edom (Jer. 9). ISIDORE. Moses, that is Christ, is found by the faithful at the river of the washing and the water of baptism, etc., down to and receiving him with religious observance they protect him.
2.9: 2.9 And when he was grown up she delivered him, etc. RABANUS. Josephus relates that Pharaoh's daughter brought the grown Moses to her father, who placed his crown upon him, which Moses at once threw down, because he saw a carved image on it. Hence the priest who was present there wished to kill him, saying that Egypt would be overthrown through him, as he had received from an oracle of demons. But Pharaoh's daughter freed him. When he was of full age, he was sent by Pharaoh against the Ethiopians. And since he knew that he would be advancing through deserts full of serpents, he took ibises, that is, Egyptian storks, and, when he had marked out a camp, he brought them forth so that they might devour and drive away the serpents: and so the army passed the night in safety. When he had come, then, to the city he was about to take, the queen of the Ethiopians fell in love with him, and according to the agreement handed the city over to him, and married him: hence it is that Aaron and Miriam quarreled against Moses because of the Ethiopian wife.
2.12: 2.12 And when he had looked about this way and that. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus. Concerning this deed of Moses we have disputed enough in that work which we wrote against Faustus on the life of the patriarchs: whether there was in him a praiseworthy disposition by which he committed this sin, as fertile land is praised for a certain wildness of useless herbs before the useful seeds; or whether the deed itself is to be justified? That it seems not, because he did not yet bear any lawful power, neither received from God nor ordained by human society: and yet, as Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles, he supposed that his brethren understood that God by his hand would give them salvation, so that by this testimony Moses seems to have been already admonished by God that he could dare this, which Scripture is silent about in that place. ISIDORE. Allegorically. Moses, that is Christ, in defending us kills the Egyptian, that is the devil, who is injurious to us in this pilgrimage, and buries the slain one in the sand. For he lies hidden in those who have no stable foundation. But he builds the Church upon the rock, and compares those who hear his word and do it to a prudent man who built his house upon firm rock. The others he compares to a fool who builds upon sand.
2.13: 2.13 And going out the next day, etc. In this Moses bore the figure of Christ, who in himself, the cornerstone, was eager to pacify the discord of the two peoples. He who did the injury and despised the reconciler is the Jewish people, who rejected the preaching of Christ the reconciler, and remained an enemy of the believing people. Hence John 9: You are his disciple; we are disciples of Moses.
2.14: 2.14 Moses feared, etc. AUGUSTINE. If the word has been so spread abroad. Two things are to be noted in this expression: namely that the sentence is left hanging and thus broken off, and then that he put the word for the deed.
2.22: 2.22 Who bore, etc. Allegorically. Christ joined to himself the Church from the Gentiles, which by the gift of the sevenfold Spirit is one in the Catholic faith. Hence: One is my dove; who bears a son who is called a stranger, and another who is God's help: for the saints are strangers upon the earth, but they never lack the help of God.
2.23: 2.23 Now after a long time, etc. After Moses took a wife in the land of Midian, the king of Egypt died: because when Christ in the world converted the nations to the faith, the principality of the devil was destroyed. Groaning. Unless the king of Egypt dies in you, you do not recognize that you are oppressed by the servitude of Egypt and the works of mud and brick; you neither groan in heart nor cry out to the Lord to free you.
3.2: 3.2 And he appeared to him. ISIDORE. Allegorically. There was a flame in the bush, and it was not consumed. The bush is the thorns of the sins of the Jews: the flame in the bush is the word of God, that is, the law given to that people. But the flame does not burn the bush, because the law given does not consume their sins. Others understand in the burning bush the Church, which is set on fire by persecutions, and which is not consumed when the Lord speaks to it. That the Lord appeared to Moses in a bush shows that he appears to the faithful in the Church, and nowhere else. The Hebrews say that God appeared to Moses in a bush so that the Jews could not carve an idol of it for themselves from there. For God always cuts off the occasion of idolatry. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 22, ch. 20. Moses, mingled with the Egyptians, was as it were awake to the world, and therefore did not hear the voice of the Lord: but when the Egyptian was slain, after he fled to the desert, while he lived there forty years, he fell asleep to earthly tumults, and therefore perceived the divine voice. For when the mind is lulled to sleep with regard to outward things, the word of God penetrates more truly. For the crowd of earthly thoughts, clamoring, shuts the ear of the heart. A man is not perfectly able for both, being divided, because if he opens his hearing outwardly, he grows deaf inwardly.
3.4: 3.4 And when the Lord saw, etc. GREGORY, Preface to the Moralia, ch. 2. The angel who is described as appearing to Moses is mentioned now as the Lord, now as an angel: an angel, because he serves by speaking outwardly; the Lord, because presiding within he gives the efficacy of speaking. For when the one speaking is ruled from within, he is mentioned as angel by his service, and as Lord by inspiration. He called him out of the midst, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 28, ch. 5. God often speaks at once to earthly and heavenly substances through angels: as here when he joined fire and bush, and united the one above with the other below. This is done only when something great is signified by the conjunction. For by speaking to Moses through the burning bush, he showed that he would become the teacher of the people, who would both receive the flame of the law and not avoid the thorn of sin: so that from that people would come one who in the fire of the Godhead would receive the sins of our flesh as the thorn of the bush, and preserve the unconsumed substance of humanity in the very flame of the divinity.
3.5: 3.5 Put off your shoes, etc. THEODORET. He commands him to take off his shoes for two reasons: first, to make him more and more religious and reverent, that he may receive his commands with trembling; and also that he be taught how the priests should minister in the tabernacle of God: for they performed the priestly office with bare feet. ISIDORE. Because no one, namely, can stand worthily or see God unless he lays aside all earthly and mortal things. Otherwise: it was the custom of the ancients that if a bridegroom repudiated his bride, he was unshod as a sign of repudiation. Therefore Moses is commanded to be unshod, and not to approach the Church, which is signified in the bush, as a bridegroom shod; for this is to be reserved to Christ, who is the true bridegroom. Of whom John says: The latchet of whose shoe I am not worthy to loose (John 1).
3.6: 3.6 I am God, etc. HILARY, On the Trinity, bk. 4. We must speak of God in no other way than as he himself has spoken of himself for our understanding. It is the angel of God who appeared in the fire from the bush: and out of the bush in the fire God speaks; you have the dispensation in the angel, because in the angel there is office, not nature; you have in the name of nature God, because the angel of God is God.
3.7: 3.7 I have seen the affliction, etc. GREGORY, Moralia. When minds are scattered outwardly it is hard for anyone to return to himself: because crooked paths hold those once caught the more pleasantly, the less it is permitted to do what one pleases. For when the duty of discipline does not stand in the way, no penalty of retribution is foreseen to terrify. But with the eyes of the heart shut the soul is hurled headlong, and it penetrates temporal evils the more securely, the more hardly it despairs of eternal goods. But this wickedness of the reprobate separates the life of the elect, like grains from the chaff, and while it afflicts, it benefits: because while it inflicts violence, it compels them to hasten to the things above; which is signified in the Israelite people, when Moses called and Pharaoh raged. For Moses was sent to call, while Pharaoh pressed them with hard works, so that one by calling might draw, the other by raging might drive, so that the people shamefully fixed in servitude might be moved, whether called or driven; this is done daily when, the heavenly rewards having been preached, the reprobate are permitted to rage against the elect: so that those whom Egypt, that is the present life, oppressed by flattering, it may help by pressing; so that while God summons, torment may drive.
18.24: 18.24 Moses did all that he had suggested, etc. A man familiar with God, most wise, not ashamed to be taught by an inferior and a Gentile, set a pattern for teachers, that they not be ashamed to be instructed by anyone.
18.26: 18.26 But whatever was more weighty, etc. AUGUSTINE, expression 88. Others: But they referred the weighty word to Moses: for so the Greek text has it, which the Latins have translated, to Moses. By that expression, indeed, the very care is figured, by which it was said upon Moses, as though a burden laid upon him is signified. A weighty word is said for a weighty question.
19.1: 19.1 In the third month, etc. ORIGEN. Another reading: In the third month of the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt: on this day they came into the desert of Sinai, and set out from Rephidim, and came into the desert of Sinai, and Israel camped there before the mountain. And Moses went up to the mount of God, and the Lord called him from the mountain, saying: Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel, etc. And a little after: Go down and testify to the people, and sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, and be ready against the third day. For on the third day the Lord will come down upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. On this day the law is found to be given, which was written on tables of stone with the finger of God, as what follows teaches. This third day appears to be of the third month from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt; from the day on which they made the Passover, that is, immolated and ate the lamb, which was the fourteenth of the first month, until this on which the law is given, fifty days are counted, seventeen namely of the first month, the rest from the fourteenth itself. Then all thirty of the second month, which make forty-seven, and the third of the third month, which is the fiftieth from the solemnity of the slain lamb; and by this, in that shadow of the future, after the day of the immolated lamb, because on the fiftieth day the law was given, written by the finger of God. So in the very truth of the New Testament, from the festival of the immolated Lamb Jesus Christ fifty days are counted, when the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, was given from on high. On this day, etc. On the forty-seventh day, namely, after they went out of Egypt, on the first day of June [sic], they came to Mount Sinai, and there, two days being completed in which they were sanctified, on the third, that is the fiftieth, they received the law: and this is Pentecost. RABANUS. In Sinai there was one station, but the greatest among all. For there the law was received, the tabernacle erected. There Exodus and the greatest part of Leviticus and almost all the books of the law were written.
19.3: 19.3 And Moses, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 6, ch. 27. Another reading: And Moses went up to the mountain, and the Lord came down to him. The mountain is the height of contemplation, to which we ascend that by gazing we may be lifted to what is beyond our weakness. But the Lord comes down, because, when the saints advance much, he opens a little of himself.
19.4: 19.4 On the wings of eagles. He calls the teachings of the two Testaments the wings of eagles, which carry us from the lowest to the heavenly.
19.6: 19.6 You shall be to me a priestly kingdom, etc. Namely, members of the high priest who is to come into the kingdom of heaven.
19.7: 19.7 He set forth all the words, etc. GREGORY. It is to be noted that the law is not thrust upon the unwary or the ignorant: but the rewards owed to those who keep it are set forth, and the past benefits which they have already experienced, and wonders, when of their own accord they devote themselves to keeping the law, the law is given to those who ask: so that according to their promise, as though liable to a vow, those who violate it may be judged, and not complain of violence done to them.
19.10: 19.10 Go to the people, etc. ORIGEN. Go down and testify to the people, and sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, and be ready against the third day, etc. Whoever wishes to come to the word of God, let him hear what the Lord commands: he must come sanctified and with washed garments. For if you bring filthy garments, it will be said to you, Matt. 22: Friend, how did you come in here not having a wedding garment? No one, therefore, can hear the word of God unless first sanctified, that is holy in body and spirit and with washed garments: for he is soon to enter to the wedding supper, to eat of the flesh of the lamb and to drink the cup of salvation. No one enters this supper in filthy garments; hence Eccles. 9: At all times let your garments be clean. For your garments have been washed once by the grace of baptism. 2 Cor. 7: You are purified in body, cleansed from all defilement of flesh and spirit. Acts 11: What God has cleansed, do not you call common. Hear the kind of sanctification: do not approach, he says, a woman today and tomorrow, that on the third day you may hear the word of God; this is what the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 7: It is good for a man not to touch a woman, saving the marriage remedy for the weak. 1 Cor. 7: But because the time is short, it remains that those who have wives be as though they had none. Sanctify them, etc. RABANUS. Whoever desires to come into the sight of God, let him sanctify himself by faith and conduct, and wash his garments, that is his works, today and tomorrow, namely in the present and in the future, that he may attain to the glory of the resurrection, which the third day hints at.
19.11: 19.11 For on the third day, etc. On this day the law was given, written on tables of stone with the finger of God; this is the third day of the third month from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. From the day on which they made the Passover, that is the fourteenth of the first month, until the law was given, fifty days are counted, seventeen namely of the first month, the rest from the fourteenth, and all thirty of the second, which are forty-seven, and the third of the third month, which is the fiftieth from the slaying of the lamb: as from the passion of Christ until the Holy Spirit is given fifty days are counted. For the finger of God signifies the Holy Spirit. ISIDORE, Questions on Exodus, ch. 28, vol. 5. On the fiftieth day after the Passover the law of Moses was given, etc., down to or because he said the truth of the law to the unbelievers through gloom, that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand (Isa. 6).
19.12: 19.12 Beware, etc. RABANUS. First he forbids the people to go up the mountain, and threatens death: now he commands that at the sounding of the trumpet they go up the mountain, restraining human audacity, and inviting to obedience: because at the voice of preaching we ought to raise ourselves to heavenly things, and not presume of our own accord by investigation of the sacraments, but follow the calling of God.
19.13: 19.13 Trumpet (buccina). As if vocina: from voice (vox), or from calling (vocare), or from the mouth (bucca).
19.14: 19.14 And when they had washed their garments, etc. It does not suffice, for the power of contemplation, to cleanse the works of penance with tears, unless chastity of mind and body follows. Hence Matt. 5: Blessed are the clean of heart, etc. And Wisdom 1: Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul.
19.18: 19.18 And all Mount Sinai was on smoke, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 6, ch. 27. The Lord, about to give the law, came down in fire and smoke, etc., down to they overcome what they are. THE SAME, Moralia, bk. 2, ch. 2. The sacred oracles at the beginning of narratives express the qualities, and the limits of causes sometimes by the position of a place, sometimes by the position of a body, sometimes by the quality of the air, etc., down to but those about to punish Sodom are recorded to have come in the evening.
19.20: 19.20 And the Lord came down, etc. THE SAME, Moralia, bk. 5, ch. 26. Moses went up, etc., down to we in some measure resound by stammering.
20.2: 20.2 I am the Lord your God. ORIGEN, Hom. 8 on Exodus. Of him who despises the present age, namely Egypt, and, translated by the word of God, is not found but hastens to the future age, God says: I am the Lord your God, etc. Not only to those who set out from Egypt, but to those who no longer serve the Egyptians, brought out of Egypt from the house of bondage (Ps. 80). The business of the world, the acts of the flesh, is a house of bondage: as to leave worldly things and live according to God is a house of freedom. Hence John 8: If you abide in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. Therefore Egypt is the house of bondage; Judea and Jerusalem, the house of liberty. Hence Gal. 4: That Jerusalem which is above is free. As therefore earthly Egypt is called a house of bondage for the children of Israel in comparison with Judea and Jerusalem, which is to them a house of freedom: so in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of freedom, the whole world and what is in it is called a house of bondage: and because from the paradise of freedom through sin we came to the bondage of the world, the first word of the decalogue is of freedom: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, etc.; this voice you will not be able to hear in Egypt. Even if it is enjoined upon you to make the Passover, gird your loins, take sandals on your feet, hold a staff in your hand, and eat unleavened bread with bitterness. But neither in the first station, nor in the second, nor in the third, nor when you have crossed the Red Sea, even if you come to the sea and bitterness is turned for you into sweetness, nor in Elim, where there were twelve fountains of water and seventy palm trees, even if you pass Rephidim and ascend the other stages, are you yet judged fit, but when you come to Mount Sinai. With difficulty, then, will you sometime deserve to receive the precepts of freedom, and hear: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Here, however, it is not a word of command, but it shows who it is that commands. The first commandment, therefore, is: You shall have no other gods before me. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus. It is asked how the ten precepts of the law are to be divided? etc., down to except that which was said: You shall have no other gods before me? ISIDORE. God gives Moses the law of our innocence and of knowledge of him, which consists in ten words, written on tables of stone with the finger of God. Three pertain to the love and knowledge of the Trinity, seven to love of neighbor, by which human society is not harmed. The first pertains to God the Father: The Lord your God is one God, that hearing this you may worship one God the Father, and not pour out fornication to many feigned gods. The second to the Son: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; that is, do not think that Christ the Son of God is a creature, because every creature is subject to vanity, but equal to the Father, God from God, light from light.
20.3: 20.3 You shall not have strange gods, etc. ORIGEN. The first commandment is: You shall have no other gods before me; and it follows: You shall not make to yourself an idol, nor any likeness, etc. Some think all these together are one commandment: but if it is counted so, the number of ten commandments will not be completed. The first commandment, therefore, is: You shall have no other gods before me, etc. The second, You shall not make to yourself an idol, nor any likeness, etc. Let us begin, then, with the first commandment: You shall have no other gods before me. If he had said, There are none, the statement would seem more absolute; but because he says, There shall not be, he did not deny that they exist, but forbade them to be for the one to whom these precepts are given. From here I think Paul took, 1 Cor. 8: For although there are those that are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth. And in other places you will find gods named, as there: A great king above all gods, and God has spoken to God, etc. Of lords the same Apostle says: Whether thrones, or dominions, etc. (Col. 1). Dominions are nothing other than a certain order and multitude of lords. In which the Apostle seems to open the sense of the law; as if he said: Though there are many lords who rule over other nations, and many gods who are worshipped by others: yet to us there is one God, and one Lord. Hence Deut. 32: When the Most High divided the nations, and separated the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. The angels, then, to whom the Most High committed the nations, Scripture calls lords or gods: gods as given by God, and lords as having obtained power from the Lord. Hence it is said to them in Psalm 81: I said: You are gods and all of you sons of the Most High. But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes; imitating, namely, the devil, who was made prince of all unto ruin. Hence it is established that transgression, not nature, made them execrable. To you therefore, O Israel, who are the portion of God and his line of inheritance, there shall be, he says, no other gods before me: because the true God is one God, and the true Lord is one Lord; to the others created by him he has given this name not by nature but by grace. These things are said not only to Israel according to the flesh, but to you who have become Israel in mind by seeing God, and circumcised in heart, not in flesh; if only you so act as to be worthy to be a portion of God and to be measured in the line of his inheritance: otherwise let them be an example to you who had been called to this, to be a portion of God, and, as their sins demanded, were scattered among all nations, and, brought out of the house of bondage, now serve not the Egyptians alone but all nations. For whoever sins is a servant of sin (John 5 [sic]).
20.4: 20.4 You shall not make, etc. ORIGEN. You shall not make to yourself an idol, nor any likeness, etc. Idols are one thing, gods another. Of gods the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 8: For although there are many gods and many lords, etc. Of idols, that an idol is nothing in the world; of likenesses he did not add, because they are nothing. Here, however, it is said: You shall not make to yourself an idol, nor any likeness. To make an idol is one thing, to make a likeness another. For example, if someone in gold and silver, wood or stone, makes the form of a quadruped, or serpent, or bird, and sets it up to be adored, he makes not an idol but a likeness. But he who makes what is not, a form namely which the eye has not seen but the mind feigns for itself; as if someone forms with human limbs the head of a dog or ram, or in one human figure two faces, or on a human breast the hind parts of a horse or fish; he who does this makes not a likeness but an idol: for he makes what is not, and has nothing like itself. Therefore the Apostle says that an idol is nothing in the world (1 Cor. 8). For no form is taken from things that exist, but what an idle and curious mind has devised. A likeness is when something is formed from the things that are either in heaven, or on earth, or in the waters: but as it is easy to speak of likenesses of things that are on earth or in the sea, so also of heavenly ones; unless someone says this can be understood of the sun, and moon, and stars, whose forms the Gentile world expresses. But Moses, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, wished to forbid even those things which were among them in secret, such as Hecate and other forms of demons, which the Apostle calls spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places (Eph. 6); of whom perhaps it is said: My sword is inebriated in heaven (Isa. 34). For by these forms and likenesses they invoked demons to repel or avoid evils. It should be known, however, that when you have decided to keep this commandment and to have only one God and Lord, this is to declare war on all others, whom you renounced in baptism, confessing God alone, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. But if confessing this we do not love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, clinging to him with all our strength, we are not made a part of the Lord, but, placed on the border, we offend those whom we flee, and do not make propitious the one to whom we flee. To such the prophet says: Woe to the double-minded (Sir. 2). And again: How long do you halt between two sides? (3 Kings 18). From those we are struck as fugitives, and by our Lord as unstable we are not defended; hence Jer. 4: Your lovers have become your enemies. There are many lovers of the soul, captured by its beauty, with whom it has played the harlot, saying: I will go after my lovers who give me my wine, etc. (Hos. 2): these it offends when it returns to its former husband. Unless, then, you remain with your husband with all faith, you are suspected on account of the crimes you have committed; he notes all your movements, glances and gait; he can see nothing wanton in you any more, nothing dissolute or prodigal. If therefore you neglect the grace received, and entangle yourself in worldly business, at once the unclean spirit returns with seven worse than himself (Matt. 12), so that he cannot be cast out again, and the last things become worse than the first. There is no fellowship, then, of the temple of God with idols. If we are God's, we ought to be such that God dwells and walks in us; hence Isa. 52: You who carry the vessels of the Lord, go out and touch not the unclean, and I will receive you, etc. He says therefore: You shall have no other gods before me.
20.5: 20.5 You shall not adore, etc. To worship (colere) is one thing, to adore another. One can adore unwillingly, either by flattering idolatrous kings, or overcome by torments, though he knows an idol is nothing. To worship is to be enslaved to them with the whole affection and zeal. He cuts off both, so that you neither worship with affection nor adore in appearance. I am the Lord, etc. See the kindness of God: to teach us and make us perfect, he does not refuse the frailty of human affections; he does and suffers all things for us, he speaks to us in known and customary affections. ORIGEN, as above. Every woman is either under a husband, and subject to the laws of the husband (Eph. 5), or is a harlot, and uses the freedom of sinning. He who goes in to a harlot knows that he has gone in to a prostitute open to all, and therefore cannot be indignant about others. He who uses lawful marriage does not suffer his wife to sin, but is kindled with zeal to preserve the chastity of marriage, that he may become a lawful father. So every soul is either prostituted to demons, and has many lovers to enter in to her, now the spirit of fornication, now avarice, after this will come the spirit of pride and very many others; yet one does not envy another, nor is moved by jealousy, but they invite one another; hence, he brings with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, etc. (Luke 11). So the soul that is prostituted to demons suffers no jealousy of its lovers; but if it is joined to a lawful husband, that is Christ, even if it has at some time been a sinner, he does not allow it to sin any more, nor can he bear that it play with adulterers; his jealousy is aroused over it, and defends the chastity of marriage; but if he sees it violating the rights of marriage, and seeking occasion to sin, he gives it a bill of divorce; hence Isa. 50: For your iniquities I put away your mother; he who speaks this is jealous and says it moved by zeal. This too is a new kind of his goodness, that even after adultery he receives the one who returns and repents with the whole heart. Hence: If a woman leave her husband and sleep with another man, shall she return to her husband? etc. And elsewhere: And after you have played the harlot in all these things, I said: Return, etc. (Jer. 3). If therefore this jealous God seeks and desires your soul to cling to him, if he guards, rebukes and is indignant, as using a kind of jealousy toward you, know that you have hope of salvation. But if you despise correction, his jealousy departs from you, according to that: Therefore my jealousy departs from you, etc. (Ezek. 16). See the mercy and piety of God; when he wishes to show mercy, he says he is indignant and angry, as he says through Jeremiah: You shall be chastised with pain and scourge, Jerusalem, that my soul depart not from you (Jer. 6). For he scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12). This is terrible, this is the last thing, if we are not corrected for our sins: for when we exceed the measure of sinning, even the jealousy of God will be taken from us, and he is angry no more. Visiting the iniquity, etc. ORIGEN. Repaying the sins of the fathers upon the children, etc. Heretics say that the saying is not of a good God, who says that one is punished for the sins of another; yet they say the God of the law is just, and cannot show how he would be unjust if he punishes one when another sins. But our inner man is said to have God as Father, if he lives according to God; or the devil, if he does his will; hence John 8: You are of your father the devil, and the desires of your father you will do. As the seed of God is in us, when keeping the word of God we do not sin, according to 1 John 3: Whoever is born of God does not sin, for his seed abides in him; so when we are persuaded by the devil to sin, we receive his seed; when we do what he persuades, he has already begotten us, for we are born his sons through sin. But because we hardly sin without help, as no one commits adultery alone, an adulteress must needs be made a partner, and if not more, some man or woman must be joined to the ministry of the crime: all of whom, as one from another, generated according to the order of persuasion, trace their offspring from the devil; as in the betrayal of the Lord the devil entered the heart of Judas, and begot the first son of sin, who could not do this alone; he went therefore to the Scribes and Pharisees and priests; there is born therefore of Judas a third generation, and a fourth, of sin. Let us see, then, how God repays the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, and not on the father himself. For nothing is said about the fathers. The devil, because he has already exceeded the measure of sinning, like a garment stiffened in blood will not be clean in this age; he is not scourged for sin; for all things are kept for him for the future. Hence Matt. 8: Have you come before the time to torment us? But the sins are repaid upon the sons whom he begot through sin, who, placed in the flesh, are scourged. God does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be rather converted and live (Ezek. 33). Being merciful, therefore, he repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons, because the devil and his angels, who are also made fathers of sin, are unworthy to be corrected in the present: their sons, and those who through them have been drawn into the fellowship of sin, receive in the present what they have done, so that, purified, they may not be made partners of the devil in punishment. Hence Psalm 88: I will visit their iniquities with a rod, etc., but my mercy I will not take away from them. For God is jealous, and does not will that the soul which he espouses in faith remain in the defilement of sin, but be quickly purged. But if it refuses to be purged, he will laugh at their destruction, saying to them, Matt. 25: Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, etc. Let us know, then, that we are corrected in the present that we may rest in the future. Hence: When we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, that we be not condemned with this world. THE SAME. On this saying heretics are wont to reproach us, that it is not the saying of a good God, who judges one for the sins of another. But those who will say that the God of the law who commands these things is not good, say nevertheless that he is just: nor can they themselves show how it would seem to agree with justice if, when one sins, another is punished. ISIDORE. The first commandment forbids stealthy deceit; the second, error; the third kills love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth, cruelty; the sixth, fornication; the seventh, rapacity; the eighth destroys falsehood; the ninth, worldly covetousness; the tenth, the thought of adultery. And it should be noted that as the Egyptians are struck with ten plagues, so the tables are written with ten precepts, by which the people of God may be ruled and demons slain. The law was written on two tables to signify the two Testaments: or because there are two precepts of love of God and neighbor, on which hang the whole law and the prophets (Matt. 22). On one are three precepts which pertain to the love of God; on the other seven, which pertain to the society of neighbor. The tables were of stone because the heart of the Jews was stony and insensible, hard and dull; hence Ezek. 36: I will take away the stony heart, and give them a heart of flesh. And the Apostle says, 2 Cor. 3: Not in tables of stone, but in the fleshly tables of the heart, which feel namely and understand.
20.12: 20.12 Honor your father, etc. This is the first of the seven commandments which pertain to the neighbor. It is fitting that there are seven. For seven consists of three and four. Three corresponds to the soul, which is irascible, concupiscible and rational. Four to the body.
20.13: 20.13 You shall not kill, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 61 on Exodus. And as to what is said, you shall not kill, it must not be thought that it is done against this precept when the law kills, or God commands someone to be killed: for he does it who commands what the minister is not permitted to refuse.
20.14: 20.14 You shall not commit adultery. ISIDORE. It is also asked how you shall not commit adultery differs from what is said a little later: You shall not covet your neighbor's wife? For in what is said, you shall not commit adultery, that could also be understood; unless perhaps in those two precepts, not to commit adultery and not to steal, the works themselves are noted, but in these last, the concupiscence itself: which differ so much that sometimes one commits adultery who does not covet his neighbor's wife, when he is joined to her for some other reason. But sometimes one covets and is not joined to her, fearing punishment: and this perhaps the law wished to show, that both are sins. THE SAME. It is also commonly asked whether fornication is included under the name of adultery, etc., down to and the non-lawful use of those members must be understood to be forbidden.
20.15: 20.15 You shall not steal, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 71 on Exodus. But again it is asked how you shall not steal differs from what is said a little later about not coveting the things of a neighbor? Not that everyone who covets the thing of a neighbor steals; but everyone who steals covets the thing of a neighbor. In that generality, where it is commanded not to covet a neighbor's goods, that which pertains to theft could also be contained.
20.16: 20.16 You shall not speak against your neighbor, etc. AUGUSTINE, as above. In what is also said, etc., down to and the like.
20.18: 20.18 And all the people saw the voices, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 72 on Exodus. It is usually asked how the people saw the voice, since a voice seems to pertain not to sight but to hearing, etc., down to hear what shines, we are not accustomed to say.
20.19: 20.19 Speak you to us, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 73. It is signified that the Old Testament pertains rather to fear, as the New to love; although in the Old the New lies hidden, and in the New the Old is laid open. How, moreover, it is granted to such a people to see the voice of God, if this is to be taken as to understand, when they fear that God speak to them lest they die, is not sufficiently clear.
20.20: 20.20 Do not fear, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 74. Thus they had to be restrained from sins, namely by fearing lest they suffer sensible punishments; because they were not yet able to love justice, and were tested by the Lord, that it might appear what kind they were; not that they might become known to God, whatever they were, from whom they were not hidden, but among themselves and to themselves.
20.21: 20.21 And the people stood, etc. GREGORY, Hom. 6. In some places of Scripture the history must be preserved, etc., down to Moses approached the dark cloud in which God was. You shall not make gods, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 76. What was said in the first precept is repeated; and by silver and gold all idols are understood, as in Psalm 113: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of men's hands.
20.24: 20.24 An altar of earth, etc. He shows that, idols being forbidden, an altar of earthly material is therefore granted, so that victims and sacrifices may be offered on it to the one God. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 3, ch. 20. To make an altar of earth to God is to hope for the incarnation of Christ. For then our gift is accepted by God, when on this altar our humility, that is, whatever it does, is placed upon faith in the Lord's incarnation. On an altar of earth, then, we place the gift offered, if we make our acts firm with faith in the Lord's incarnation.
20.25: 20.25 Of hewn stones. ISIDORE. Hewn stones are those who cut unity, and divide themselves from the society of the brethren: these Christ does not receive into his body, whose body the construction of the altar signifies by figure. The unhewn stones of which the altar is commanded to be built are those who are made solid in unity through faith; of whom it is said, 1 Peter 2: You are living stones, built up into spiritual houses. Iron has not been laid on these, because they are uncorrupted, and have not received the fiery darts of the evil one: all make one altar in the unity of faith and the concord of charity.
21.1: 21.1 These are the judgments, etc. AUGUSTINE, expression 91 on Exodus. What pertains to the neighbor is henceforth explained more distinctly; note the expression, since it was said to Moses: These are the judgments which you shall set before them; the rest are said to the people. If you buy a Hebrew servant, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 77 on Exodus. Lest Christians demand this here from their masters, the apostle commands servants to be subject to their masters (1 Pet. 2), lest the name of the Lord and the teaching be blasphemed: for it is clear from this that the precept is in a mystery, because God commanded that the ear of the one who refused liberty be pierced with an awl against the doorpost. GREGORY, Hom. 3 on Ezekiel, vol. 2. It should be known that, since the active and contemplative life are from the grace of God, etc., down to because that inner rest is seen in an enigma. Six years. ISIDORE. Serving in the six ages of this world, on the seventh day, that is the eternal sabbath, we shall be freed, if we have been willing to be free while in this world we serve sin. But if we are unwilling, the ear will be pierced as a testimony of disobedience, and with our wife and sons, whom we preferred to freedom, that is with the flesh and its works, we shall serve sin forever.
21.7: 21.7 If a man sell his daughter, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 78 on Exodus. She shall not go out as handmaids go out, etc., down to it is understood that she will go out with him free, not separated from her husband.
21.13: 21.13 But he who did not lie in wait, etc. RABANUS, on Exodus, vol. 2. For involuntary homicides, etc., down to has placed [in?] Christ, shall be safe. AUGUSTINE, Question 79 on Exodus. But if he did not will it, but God delivered him into his hands, etc. This is said in this way, etc., down to and Judas therefore justly betrayed.
21.18: 21.18 If men quarrel, etc. RABANUS. It is the same if someone, contending with his neighbor, has exasperated him through hardness of mind or stinginess, namely by scorning or by not taking counsel; and he, weakened by sadness, has languished from the fervor of love: let the guilty one, through confession, devote the labor of penance and the expense of promised amendment to physicians, that is teachers, who may raise the weak one with the staff of consolation and restore him with the fomentations of preaching to the former state of love. In correction discretion is necessary, lest he who ought to correct kill, or send to despair or hatred.
21.22: 21.22 If men quarrel. THE SAME. If someone injures the soul of another, after the conception of the word, through carelessness or fraud, so that the vital germ of a good work cannot bring forth sound: even if that soul, still living in faith, has persisted, he will be obliged, according to the ministry of the Gospel, to restore the damage inflicted through penance.
