But if the soul itself, killed through error, after the abortion has been brought forth, that is a deadly work, has persevered in unbelief, without doubt its seducer, as a true murderer, will be guilty of eternal death. AUGUSTINE, Question 80 on Exodus. That he did not wish the unformed offspring to pertain to homicide, etc., down to and therefore not yet endowed with senses. ORIGEN, Hom. 10 on Exodus. But if two men quarrel, and strike a pregnant woman, and her child come forth not yet formed, he shall suffer damage, as much as the woman's husband shall demand, and he shall give for his life. But if it was formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, etc. First let us see about the one who came forth not yet formed, how one of the quarrelers is commanded to be struck with loss of money, when two are mentioned. What is also this that the woman's husband imposes it upon him, and not upon them; and he shall give, and not rather they shall give. But if the child has come forth already formed, we easily understand giving life for life: namely, the sin is avenged by death. But what follows it is worth the trouble to explain. For it does not seem that even a formed child, struck by the kick of a quarreler, lost an eye in the womb, and certainly had no teeth. For if we refer this to the mother, how does a miscarrying woman lose an eye, or suffer pain in her teeth? But granted that, struck in the eye or in a tooth, she miscarried, she received a bruise or a wound, what then do we say about burning for burning? Could the woman, standing by the quarreling men, have been burned, that burning be paid for burning? In Deuteronomy also these things cannot easily be explained. In the same Scriptures, however, the members of the soul are named by the same words and offices which the members of the body use or are called by. Hence Matt. 7: You see the mote in your brother's eye, and the beam that is in your own eye you do not see. And Matt. 13: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. And Rom. 10: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace! Let not the similarity of words, therefore, disturb us. There are, then, two quarreling, two disputing with dogmas or questions of the law, and wrangling about battles of words; hence the Apostle, 2 Tim. 2: Do not contend in words, etc. And in the same place: Avoid questions of the law, knowing that they beget strife. Those therefore who quarrel in these questions to the subversion of the hearers strike the pregnant woman, and cast out the formed or still unformed child. The pregnant woman is said to be the soul which has lately conceived the word of God; hence: From your fear, Lord, we have conceived in the womb and have brought forth (Isa. 26). Those, then, who conceive and at once bring forth are not to be thought women, but men and perfect; hence elsewhere: If the earth has brought forth in one day, and a nation is born at once in one day (Isa. 66). This is therefore the generation of the perfect, which is conceived and born on the same day. Men bring forth, according to Gal. 4: My little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you. The perfect and men, therefore, bring forth at once, that is, bring the conceived word of faith into works: but the soul which conceives and retains in the womb and does not bring forth is called woman. Hence Isa. 37: The pains of childbirth have come upon her: and there is no strength to bring forth. This soul, therefore, while the two quarrel among themselves and put forth scandals, is struck and scandalized: so that it casts away the word of faith, which it had feebly conceived, not yet formed. For in some the word is formed, in others not formed; hence: Until Christ be formed in you (Gal. 4); for Christ is the Word of God. He will therefore suffer damage who caused the miscarriage. Of damages the Apostle speaks of the teacher in 1 Cor. 3: If any man's work burn, he shall suffer loss, etc. And the Lord himself in the Gospel, Matt. 16: What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Hence it seems to be shown that some sins pertain to loss, but not to destruction, because he who has suffered loss is said to be saved, yet so as by fire: hence John says some sins are unto death, some not (1 John 5). But which are unto death cannot easily be discerned. Who understands sins? (Ps. 18). But when five other minas are gained over five minas, and two over two (Luke 19), he who loses the reward of this gain is said to be struck with loss, as is he who has given cause of scandal to a weaker and womanly soul. He shall give according as the husband shall demand, and he shall give with honor to the learning soul. The husband is the master Christ, or he who for Christ is a teacher of souls. He will suffer loss, therefore, who contends to the subversion of the hearers, for the soul which had not yet had a formed child: which can be taken of the scandal of a catechumen. It can also happen that he who injured instructs and repairs for the soul what he destroyed, and with honor, namely with modesty, with meekness, not with strife, as when he brought scandal. But when the child has been formed, he shall give life for life. The formed child can be taken as the word of God in the heart of the soul that has received the grace of baptism, or one who has received the word of God more evidently and clearly. The one who struck will render, therefore, life for life on the day of judgment, namely before that judge who can destroy soul and body in hell. Or that he who is conscious to himself of such a scandal may lay down his life for the life of the scandalized, and even to death give labor how he may be restored to the faith. Let him lay down eye for eye: if he injured the eye of the soul, that is, disturbed its understanding, let his eye be taken from him by the one who presides over the Church, that is his understanding. If he injured a tooth, which, receiving the food of the word of God, used to crush it or grind it with the molars, so as to send a subtle sense to the belly of the soul: if he has troubled and pulled out this tooth, so that by its crushing the soul cannot subtly and spiritually receive the word of God, his tooth will be taken away, who did not well crush and divide the foods of the word. For on this account perhaps it is said of the Lord: You have broken the teeth of sinners (Ps. 3). And elsewhere: The Lord will break the molars of the lions (Ps. 57). So by members the soul is said to be injured and struck. He also demands hand for hand, and foot for foot. The hand of the soul is the power by which it can hold something and grasp the heart, as its action and strength; and the foot by which it walks toward good or evil. Because therefore the scandalized soul is cast down not only in faith but also in acts, which are signified by the hands, his hands are taken away, with which he does not work well, and his feet, with which he does not walk well. He shall also receive burning, because he burned and handed the soul over to hell. By each of these it is shown that the striker, all his members being cut off, is cut off from the body of the Church, that others seeing may have fear and not do likewise. Therefore the Apostle, when he describes the teacher of the Church, commands among other things: not a striker (1 Tim. 3): lest, striking pregnant women, that is foolish souls, he lay down life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, etc. Of such it is said, Matt. 24: Woe to those who are with child and who nurse in those days, in which even the elect, if it were possible, shall be scandalized. It should be known, however, that to be scandalized is not for the perfect but for women or little ones; hence Matt. 18: Whoever shall scandalize one of these little ones, etc.
21.29: 21.29 But if the ox was wont to push with his horn, etc. RABANUS. That is, if the master, that is the spirit, does not restrain a proud motion of the mind, and it brings destruction to souls or inconvenience to bodies, the guilt overflows upon the keeper. Hence Proverbs chapter 16: The heart of the wise man will instruct his mouth, and will add grace to his lips. Thirty shekels. That is, according to the commands of the law, he will make amends through faith and hope and charity. Of silver. He will compensate for the brightness of the divine word, in which they had been instructed in the faith of the Trinity and the knowledge of the decalogue. If any man open, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 17, ch. 13. To open a pit is to penetrate the secrets of Sacred Scripture with a vigorous understanding, etc., down to whence the weakness of the hearers may slip down to the depths. If another's ox, etc. AUGUSTINE. This is not to be observed in the ox alone, but in every beast; for the whole is understood from the part. But this cannot be done with the flesh of the slain animal, which they do not eat.
22.1: 22.1 If anyone steal, etc. STRABO. According to the letter, five oxen are restored for one ox, and four sheep for one sheep: because an ox has five uses, a sheep four. For the ox is sacrificed, plows, feeds, gives milk, and its hide serves various uses; the sheep is sacrificed, and feeds, and gives milk and wool. Allegorically, by the ox any Jew is understood, whom if a Jew sells he will be subject to the penalty of the law, which is contained in the five books of Moses. By the sheep a Christian, who imitates Christ, of whom it is said: He was led as a sheep to the slaughter (Isa. 53). If anyone sells him, let him restore four sheep, that is, let him do penance according to the institution of the four Gospels.
22.2: 22.2 If a thief break open a house, or dig through it, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 84 on Exodus. If a thief be found digging through and be struck and die, etc., down to for now he is more than a thief.
22.6: 22.6 If a fire break out, etc. RABANUS. We kindle a fire when we prepare correction for subordinates, that we may consume the thorns of vices. But care must be taken lest when we pursue vices we harm virtues, and injure those who had begun to bring forth the fruit of good works before maturity. He who has done this, therefore, should perform fitting penance, and zealously restore what he injured through inertia. Ears of corn. Tender hearers not yet reaching the maturity of fruit: whose vices he who rebukes harshly and indiscriminately sends, as it were, fire among the ears of corn, and does not allow them to come to maturity.
22.14: 22.14 He who from his neighbor, etc. We ask a loan from the neighbor when for eternal recompense we undertake the care of the Lord's flock. But if we always set the fear of God before the eyes of the heart, as of one demanding money, we are always as in his presence. Hence 2 Cor. 5: Knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade men. And elsewhere, 2 Cor. 12: As before God, in Christ we speak. The death or weakness of the beast, therefore, is not imputed to the shepherd, if he has performed its care strenuously, and as with God present; otherwise he is compelled to make restitution. Hence Matt. 5: You shall not go out from thence till you pay the last farthing.
22.17: 22.17 If the father of the maid, etc. RABANUS. The sense of the sentence is historical, out of which the discourse arises. If therefore the historical sense builds up the kingdom of charity and destroys that of covetousness, it is not necessary to explain it allegorically. The reader, however, should honor the sentence with the dowry of right faith and leave it untouched by his exposition.
22.18: 22.18 You shall not suffer sorcerers to live. Those who act by the tricks of magic art and diabolical fabrications, understand as heretics, who are to be excommunicated from the company of the faithful who truly live, until the sorcery of error dies in them.
22.21: 22.21 You shall not afflict a stranger. RABANUS. He commends love of neighbor through compassion of mercy, lest, moved by a spur of rage or avarice, we neglect the law of nature. But what we wish men to do to us, let us do the same to them, and what we do not wish done, let us not do.
3.8: 3.8 And to bring them out of that land, etc. GREGORY, Hom. 32. Something about the present life had to be promised to a rude people, so that they might be more strongly established in the future. For if they did not receive small things, they would not believe great ones. God therefore, by bestowing earthly things, persuades also to heavenly ones, so that, receiving what they saw, they might hope for what they did not see. Into a good and spacious land, a land that flows with milk, etc. Ibid. Present prosperity is sometimes given to call to a better life, sometimes to condemn more fully for eternity. Hence the land of Canaan is promised to the Israelites, so that at some time they may be called to hope for eternal things: because a rude people would not believe the promises unless they received something near at hand from the one who promised. Therefore a man is drawn not only by hope to things, but sometimes by things to hope. Hence Psalm 104: And he gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples, that they might keep his justifications and seek his law.
3.14: 3.14 He who is has sent me to you, etc. Moses is sent to Pharaoh to punish him and finally to kill him: the law was sent to destroy the devil. Jerome, writing to Marcella on the ten names of God, puts in the sixth place the name Ehieh, which is read in Exodus: He who is has sent me to you. For God alone, who has no beginning, holds the name of true being: which was spoken by the angel to Moses when he asked his name, because in comparison with him who truly is, since he is unchangeable, the things that are changeable are as if they were not; for what is said, it was, is not; and what is said, it will be, is not yet. But God only is, who knows neither having been nor going to be. And the Father alone with the Son and the Holy Spirit truly is. Compared with his essence, our being is not; hence also we say: God lives, because the divine essence lives a life which death does not have.
3.17: 3.17 To a land flowing with milk and honey, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 4 on Exodus. Are we to take this spiritually, because in the strict sense the land that was given to the Hebrews was not such? Or is it a manner of speaking by which the fertility and sweetness of the land are praised?
3.21: 3.21 You shall not go out, etc. AUGUSTINE, ibid. As to what the Lord commanded the Hebrews, that they should take from the Egyptians vessels of silver and gold, and clothing, and added, and you shall spoil them, no unjust judgment can be made of this command. For it is God's command, about which one is not to judge but to obey. For he knows how justly he commanded; it belongs to a servant to do obediently what he has commanded.
3.22: 3.22 Vessels of silver. We ask silver and gold from the Egyptians, with which to fabricate a tabernacle for God, when we read poets and philosophers, so that we may expound divine Scripture more wisely and eloquently.
4.2: 4.2 What is that, etc. GREGORY. Moses is the Jewish people; the rod, the power of the Godhead; the serpent, the mortality of Christ: for death is signified through a serpent, and mortality through a serpent. Or because it is written, Matt. 10: Be wise as serpents; and because the highest wisdom, that is, the Wisdom of God, was incarnate: rightly is his mortality figured in the serpent. Hence John 3: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up. Moses held a rod: because the Jewish people before the coming of the Redeemer trusted in the power of God; he cast it on the ground, because through the patriarchs and prophets it announced that God would become incarnate; the rod is turned into a serpent, because Christ, God remaining in himself, was made mortal in man. But Moses also, seeing the serpent, was greatly afraid and fled, because the Jewish people, when it saw Christ mortal, feared to believe him God. He is commanded to take it by the tail, because the people which now refuses to believe, in the last part of the Lord's body, that is, in the later time of the Church, namely at the end of the world, will gather itself to the faith; holding the tail of the serpent, because him whom it had formerly despised as mortal it will confess in the last part of the Church as its Redeemer. Soon the serpent returns into a rod, because when the Jewish people has believed in Christ, soon he will appear for judgment in the power of his divinity: so that now the serpent is a rod: because he who on earth was a despised man, coming from heaven will be seen as God above the angels. ISIDORE. The serpent persuaded man to death. Death therefore is from the serpent; the rod in the serpent is Christ in death. Moses was afraid and fled: for when Christ was dead the disciples were afraid, withdrawing from the hope in which they had been. He took it by the tail, that is, by the hinder parts, and it became a rod: because having first been slain, afterward, all things being accomplished, he returned by rising again to what he had been, where, death being swallowed up by life, nothing of the serpent appeared in him. Or the tail of the serpent is the end of the age, because thus the mortality of the Church rolls on through slippery times; some go, others come through death, as through the serpent by which death was sown: but at the end of the age, as at the tail, we return to the hand of God, and, being seized, we shall be restored, and, the last enemy death being destroyed, rising again we shall be the rod of the kingdom in the right hand of God.
4.6: 4.6 Put your hand, etc. PROCOPIUS. Some assert that this portent happened to show that the law is not laid down for the just man. Although he afterwards enacts laws as to how the disease of leprosy is to be examined and the person pronounced unclean, yet most laws are delivered as though given to fools and infants. So much does God accommodate himself to our weakness! ISIDORE. The hand white, that is, unclean, for whiteness in the skin is leprosy, not brightness. For the very inheritance of God, that is the people, being sent out from him, was made unclean. Hence Psalm 73: Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand, etc. But the hand was called back into the bosom, and returned to its color: so the Jewish people, estranged from the bosom of God, remained outside unclean; but when called back, it will return to its former color, when it has recognized the Savior. For blindness in part has happened in Israel (Rom. 11).
4.9: 4.9 Take water, etc. ISIDORE. Water signifies the people; hence Apoc. 17: The waters which you saw are peoples and nations. The people, therefore, is turned into blood, that is, into faith in the blood of Christ.
4.10: 4.10 I beseech you, Lord, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus. When Moses says to the Lord: I pray, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday and the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant, it is understood that he believes it possible for one to be made suddenly eloquent by the will of God, when he says: nor since you began to speak to your servant, as though showing that it could happen that one who had not been eloquent yesterday and the day before might suddenly become so from the time the Lord began to speak with him. ORIGEN, Hom. 3 on Exodus. While Moses was in Egypt and was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he was not thin of voice, nor slow of tongue, nor did he profess himself ineloquent. For he was, as far as the Egyptians were concerned, of a sonorous voice and incomparable eloquence. But when he heard the voice of God and received the words of the Lord, he feels his voice to be thin and slight and slow and his tongue hindered, and declares himself mute, when he begins to know the true Word, which was in the beginning with God (John 1): for though an uneducated man be compared with mute animals he will seem eloquent; but if with the learned and eloquent, foolish and mute. But if anyone looks to the word of God and divine wisdom, hanging far more than with us, before God he will declare himself a mute animal. Hence Psalm 72: I am become as a beast before you. Because, then, he advanced to such understanding that he knew himself, which is a great part of wisdom, the divine condescension rewarded him, saying: I will open your mouth, etc. Blessed are they whose mouth God opens that they may speak. Hence Psalm 80: Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it. Likewise Paul says, Eph. 6: That speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth. Of those, therefore, who speak true things, God opens the mouth: of those who speak a lie, false witness, buffooneries, baseness, and also of whisperers and detractors, and of those who speak idle things, the devil opens the mouth. Of Judas it is related, John 13, that Satan entered into him, and put it into his heart to betray him. He opened his mouth, therefore, that he might speak with the Pharisees, how he would betray him for the money received. It is no small grace to discern the mouth which God opens and the one which the devil opens. God also opens the ears of the saints to hear divine words; hence: The Lord will open my ear. He opens the eyes, as he opened Hagar's eyes, and she saw a well of living water; hence Elisha: Open, Lord, the eyes of your servant, that he may see, for there are more with us (4 Kings 6). But the ear which is opened by the instruction of the Lord is sometimes open, sometimes shut; hence: Do not receive a vain hearing (Sir. 45 [sic]). If vain, profane, base things are said, he who knows the instruction of the Lord shuts his ear and says: But I, as a deaf man, did not hear, and as a mute who does not open his mouth (Ps. 37). But if what is said pertains to the profit of the soul, if the talk is of God, if it teaches morals, invites to virtues, cuts off vices, let the ears lie open and the whole door of the soul. It should be noted that the law used the greatest moderation in saying: You shall not receive a vain hearing; it did not say, You shall not hear, but, You shall not receive. For we often hear vain things: Marcion and Valentinus, and all who dispute against the Creator, speak vain things; yet we frequently hear them in order to contradict, but we do not receive them, because the devil opens their mouth. May the Lord deign to open our mouth, that we may be able to refute the one who contradicts, and stop the mouth which the devil opens.
4.11: 4.11 Who made the mouth of man? etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 8. There are those who slander God, or rather the Scripture of the Old Testament, because God said that he made the mute. What then do they say of Christ plainly saying, John 10: I came that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind? And who, unless ignorant, would believe that anything could happen to a man according to bodily defects that God does not will? But no one doubts that he wills it all justly.
4.12: 4.12 Go therefore, etc. AUGUSTINE. Allegorically. When the Lord says to Moses: But now go, and I will open your mouth and teach you what you shall speak, it appears that not only the instruction of the mouth but also the very opening pertains to the grace of God. For he does not say, Open your mouth, and I will instruct you; but promises both, I will open, and I will instruct. In Psalm 80, moreover: Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it. Here it signifies in man the will to receive what God gives to one who wills, so that Open your mouth wide pertains to the beginning of the will, but And I will fill it to the grace of God.
4.14: 4.14 The Lord, angry with Moses, said, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 10 on Exodus. He seems as though he did not give the fullest ability to one who was diffident, etc., down to whose figure Moses bears as being in the middle between God and Aaron, and Aaron between Moses and the people.
4.15: 4.15 And I will be in your mouth and in his mouth, etc. ORIGEN. It is promised not only to Moses that his mouth shall be opened by the Lord, but also to Aaron. For it is said: I will open your mouth and his mouth, and will teach you what you shall do.
4.19: 4.19 The Lord therefore said, etc. AUGUSTINE, Expressions in Genesis, vol. 3 [sic]. But after many days the king of Egypt died. And the Lord said to Moses in Midian: Go, depart into Egypt, etc. Many kinds of expression are to be noted in these words. First he says: Go, depart into Egypt, as though one were not enough; then, all are dead who sought your life, although Scripture has said that only the king of Egypt died: of whom alone it had been said before that he sought to kill Moses: or did he die last, after the other enemies? If so, it is not an expression but the sense.
4.20: 4.20 Moses therefore took, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 12 on Exodus. As to what is said, that Moses set his wife and his children upon a beast of burden, to go into Egypt: but afterwards Jethro his father-in-law met him there with them, when he had brought the people out of Egypt; it must be understood that after that killing which was to be done by the angel, the wife of Moses, or of the child, returned with the little ones. For some have thought that the angel frightened him on this account, lest the female sex should accompany him to the hindrance of the ministry divinely laid upon him.
4.21: 4.21 I will harden his heart. AUGUSTINE, Sermon 88. What is, I will harden his heart, but that when my grace is absent, his own wickedness hardens him? As often as water is bound by excessive cold, it is dissolved when the heat of the sun comes; and when the sun departs it hardens again: so by the cold of sins the charity of many grows cold, and they are hardened like ice; and when the heat of divine mercy comes upon them, they are dissolved. We recognize this in Pharaoh, who as often as the scourges were removed, hardened himself and rose up against God; as often as he was afflicted, he made supplication. There is therefore no injustice in God. Hence it was not so much the power as the patience of God that made Pharaoh harden. A thing which we also are accustomed to practice with our household servants, whom, when they sin often, we indulge, saying: I made you such; by sparing you I have nourished your insolence and negligence.
4.24: 4.24 The Lord met him, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 11 on Exodus. Another reading: And it happened on the way, at the lodging, that an angel met him, and sought to kill him: and Zipporah, taking a flint, circumcised the foreskin of her son, and fell at his feet and said: The blood of my child's circumcision has stood, and he departed from him because she said: The blood of circumcision has stood. First it is asked whom the angel wished to kill, etc., down to a great sacrament, if I am not mistaken.
4.25: 4.25 A bloody husband you are, etc. According to the history, a Gentile mother, wondering at the strangeness of the matter, could say to Moses: A bloody husband you are to me; as if to say, the rite of your nation forces me to shed the blood of my son, which is not the custom among other nations. Mystically, however, Zipporah signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which strips the foreskin of her son, that is, of the Gentile people, with a very sharp rock, that is, the teaching of the Holy Spirit, or that rock of which it is said, 2 Cor. 10 [sic]: And the rock was Christ, that it may be cleansed from all defilement of flesh and spirit: And put off the old man with his deeds (Col. 3). For the blood of circumcision stands when this corruptible shall put on incorruption.
4.27: 4.27 And the Lord said, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 32 [sic]. Aaron met Moses, and went out of Egypt. But it matters where he meets Moses, whose mouth is to be opened by the Lord: he meets him in the mountain of God. Rightly is his mouth opened who meets him in the mountain of God. Peter, James and John deserved to see on the mountain the Lord Jesus transfigured, and Moses and Elijah with him in glory. You too, unless you ascend the mountain of God, and there meet Moses, that is, unless you climb the lofty ascent of the law, unless you take possession of the summit of spiritual understanding, the door is not opened by the Lord. If you stand in the lowly place of the letter, you have not met Moses on the mountain of God; God has not opened your mouth, nor taught what you ought to speak; unless Aaron had met Moses on the mountain, unless he had seen his lofty sense, he would not have spoken to him the words of God, nor handed over the power of signs, nor made him a sharer in so great a mystery.
5.1: 5.1 Let my people go. ORIGEN, Hom. 3 on Exodus. Moses does not want the people, set in Egypt, to serve God there, but to go out into the desert and serve there. For while someone remains in the dark acts of the world and is occupied in the obscurity of business, he cannot serve God. For you cannot serve God and mammon (Matt. 6). We must therefore go out of Egypt: let each one leave the world, not in place but in mind, if we wish to serve the Lord. Hence John says: Little children, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world (1 John 2).
5.2: 5.2 Who is the Lord? He expresses the pride of the devil, who, scorning to be subject to God, says: I will be like the Most High (Isa. 14); and as if doubting the Lord's birth, says: If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread (Matt. 4). But afterwards the demons cried out as though compelled: Why have you come before the time to torment us? We know that you are the Son of God (Matt. 8). After torments they know what before they did not wish to know. Pharaoh too, when beaten, asks that supplication be made for him to the Lord. Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice? etc. You see what crude pride does; you will see a little later how much he profits by the scourges: how much better he is made when beaten; he who now says, I do not know the Lord, when beaten will say: Pray the Lord for me. Let no one therefore be so unlearned in divine discipline as to think the divine scourges ruin and penal destruction. Behold, even Pharaoh, most hard, profits when beaten: for before the blows he does not know the Lord, and when beaten he asks that supplication be made for him; and advancing in punishments, he knows to acknowledge why he is punished. I do not know, he says, the Lord. In the Gospel the one beaten corrects this voice, because the demons cried out: We know who you are: you are the Son of the living God. After the scourges he will even let Israel go, and will even urge them to leave. For there is no fellowship of light with darkness, no part of the believer with the unbeliever (2 Cor. 6).
5.3: 5.3 The God of the Hebrews has called us, etc. AUGUSTINE on Exodus. The question is how it is said to the people, etc., down to that a just judgment may follow. ORIGEN. Morally. We set out on a three days' journey from Egypt if we so preserve ourselves from all defilement of soul, body and spirit that our spirit, soul and body are kept whole until the day of Christ. ORIGEN. We set out on a three days' journey from Egypt if, taking rational, moral and natural wisdom away from worldly things, we turn them to divine institutions. We set out on a three days' journey from Egypt if, purifying in ourselves words, deeds and thoughts (for these three are the ways in which men can sin), we are made clean of heart, that we may be able to see God. But the prince of Egypt, when he sees himself pressed more vehemently to let the people of God go, in the second place desires to obtain that they not go far away, lest they set out the whole three days, saying: Do not go far away. He does not want the people of God to be made far from him. For he wants them, if not in deed, to sin in word; if not in word, in thought. He does not want them to depart from him the whole three days. He wants to possess in us one day at least, in others two, in others the whole three days. Blessed are those who depart from him the whole three days. A journey of three days into the wilderness, and let us sacrifice to God, etc. ISIDORE. We walk a three days' journey going out of Egypt, that we may come to the place where we ought to sacrifice to the Lord. This way is Christ, who says, John 14: I am the way, the truth and the life. For whoever shall confess Christ with the mouth, and believe in the heart that God raised him on the third day, shall be saved, coming to the place in which the sacrifice of praise is offered. STRABO. A journey of three days, etc. At the third stage, after they had crossed the Red Sea, they came to Etham, which place is also called Marah, on account of the bitter waters. Or of three days, that is, of three months, because in the third month after they went out of Egypt they came to Sinai, where they sacrificed and received the law, where also the tabernacle was erected. ORIGEN, Hom. 3 on Exodus. Now also Moses, whom we have with us (for we have Moses and the prophets), that is, the law of God, wishes to lead you out of Egypt, if you hear it; he wishes to make you far from Pharaoh, to rescue you from the work of mud and straw: if only you hear and understand spiritually; he does not want you to remain in the acts of the flesh and of darkness, but to go out to the wilderness, to a place namely empty of the disturbances and billows of the world, and to the quiet of silence. For the words of wisdom are learned in silence and quiet. In this place you will be able to sacrifice to the Lord the law of God, and to recognize the power of the divine voice. Therefore Moses desires to cast you out of the waves of business and the clamor of peoples, and out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of ignorance, that you may hear the law of God and take hold of the light of knowledge.
5.4: 5.4 Why do you, Moses and Aaron, call off, etc. ORIGEN, ibid. While the people are with him, and work mud or brick, while they are busy with straw, he does not think them perverse, but walking rightly. But if they say, We wish to go a journey of three days and serve the Lord, he says the people are being perverted by Moses and Aaron. Today also, if Moses and Aaron, that is, prophetic and priestly speech, stir the soul to the service of God, to go out of the world, to renounce all that it possesses, to attend to the law and word of God: you will immediately hear the like-minded friends of Pharaoh saying: See how men are seduced and young men perverted, so that they do not labor, do not serve in the army, do not do anything useful, and, leaving necessary things, pursue trifles and idleness. What is it to serve God? They do not want to work and look for occasions of leisure: these were then the words of Pharaoh, and these his friends speak now, and they persecute not only with words but with blows. He orders the scribes of the Hebrews to be flogged, straw not to be given, the work to be exacted; the fathers suffered these things, and the people of God suffer them now. Those who have handed themselves over entirely to the prince of this world prosper; everything, as they think, turns out happily: but for the servants of God even a small and humble livelihood does not succeed. These are the straws that were given by Pharaoh; hence some, wearied, say to Pharaoh: Why do you afflict your people? For overcome by blows they fall from the faith, and confess that they are Pharaoh's people, for not all who are of Israel are Israelites.
5.9: 5.9 Let them be oppressed with works and fulfill them, etc. Mystically. From the time Moses began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God are the more afflicted: from the time the word of God reaches the soul, the devil rises up more fiercely and sends in greater vices. For before the word of God came to rebuke the vices, they lasted in peace, but when it comes, a great disturbance arises.
5.14: 5.14 And they were scourged who, etc. The children of Israel were more grievously worn down after they resolved to go out of Egypt; because those who wish to renounce the world and wicked works are assailed by the devil with fiercer temptations.
5.21: 5.21 May the Lord see, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 29, ch. 14. When the divine light illuminates the human heart, it grieves to the point of seeming to stink in the eyes of Pharaoh. Because you have made our odor to stink, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 3. Allegorically. They speak truth, although they do not know it, like Caiaphas, who said: It is expedient that one man should die for the people (John 18); he did not know what he said. For as the Apostle says: We are the good odor of Christ, to some unto life, to others unto death, so the prophetic word is a sweet odor to believers; but to the doubtful and unbelieving, and those who confess themselves the people of Pharaoh, it is made an execrable odor. Moses himself also says to the Lord: Since I have spoken to Pharaoh, you have afflicted your people; because before the word of God is heard there is no tribulation or temptation: but when the trumpet of preaching has shown the signal of war, the battle of tribulations arises. From the time, therefore, that Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God are afflicted. From the time the word of God is brought forth in your soul, a contest is stirred up within you of the virtues against the vices, which before lasted within you in peace. But when the word of God has begun to make a division in each person, a great disturbance arises, and war is born without treaty: because injustice does not agree with justice, nor drunkenness with sobriety, nor falsehood with truth. Therefore let us not be disturbed if we seem an execrable odor to Pharaoh. For virtue is called the execration of vice. But as Moses stood before Pharaoh, let us also stand; let us not bend, having our loins girt about with truth, and our feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace (Eph. 6). Let us stand confidently, and pray the Lord to set our feet upon a firm rock, that our feet be not moved. Let us stand, that is, resist, according to 1 Pet. 5: Whom resist, strong in faith: that Satan may soon be crushed under our feet. For the more constantly and bravely we stand, the weaker Pharaoh is. But if we begin to be weak or doubtful, he will become stronger. For when Moses raised his hands, Amalek was conquered; when he let them down as if weary, Amalek prevailed. Let us therefore in the power of the cross of Christ lift up our arms, and raise holy hands in prayer, that we may deserve the help of God. Hence James says: Resist the devil and he will flee from you (James 3 [sic]). Let us act, therefore, so that he not only flees but is crushed under our feet, destroyed in the depth of the abyss. But if we depart from the Egypt of vices, we pass over the waves of the world as a solid road through Jesus Christ.
5.22: 5.22 Lord, why have you afflicted this people? AUGUSTINE. These are not words of stubbornness or indignation, but of inquiry and prayer, as appears from what the Lord answered. For he does not rebuke his unbelief, but reveals what he is about to do.
6.3: 6.3 And my name Adonai I did not make known to them. As to you. For through the successions of ages the increase of divine knowledge grew. The Lord appeared to Abraham; he spoke face to face with Moses; but David says in Psalm 118: I have understood more than the aged, etc. The Apostles beheld the Son of God present, and asked whatever they wished, to whom also it is said, Luke 2 [sic]: Many kings and prophets, etc.
6.7: 6.7 From the workhouse of the Egyptians. Ergastulum, and ergasterium, that is, a place of work: namely where the guilty were bound to do works.
6.9: 6.9 They did not agree with him, etc. Note the mercy of God: he is not believed by the children of Israel, and yet he does not cease to admonish. He is despised by Pharaoh, and patiently waits.
6.12: 6.12 Behold the children, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 16 on Exodus 70 [sic]. Behold, I am of a thin voice, and how will Pharaoh hear me? He does not seem, however, to excuse himself about the thinness of his voice because of the multitude of the people, but also because of one man: it is a wonder if his voice was so thin that it could not be heard even by one. Or perhaps royal pride did not allow them to speak from nearby.
6.14: 6.14 These are the princes, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 15. Wishing to show the origin of Moses, as his action required, Scripture begins from the firstborn of Jacob, that is, Reuben; thence to Simeon, thence to Levi: it goes no further, because Moses is from Levi. These, however, are mentioned who had already been mentioned among those seventy-five with whom Israel had entered into Egypt. For God willed that not the first or the second but the third tribe, that is the Levitical, should be the priestly one.
6.20: 6.20 And Amram took Jochebed, etc. STRABO. Amram is interpreted a high father, which signifies Christ; Jochebed, the grace of God, which signifies the Church: from Christ and the Church is born Moses, that is, the spiritual law, and Aaron, namely the true priesthood. And he took, etc. She was of the tribe of Judah, sister of Nahshon, who was prince of the tribe of Judah in the desert: for it had not yet been commanded that each should take a wife from his own tribe. These tribes, the Levitical and the royal, were already then joined, so that it might be understood that Christ, king and priest, was to come from them.
6.21: 6.21 And the sons of Izhar, etc. STRABO. It is asked why Korah, whom the earth swallowed alive for his iniquity, is written in the genealogy of the just? But it signifies that heretics will be with Catholics in the Church.
6.27: 6.27 This Moses. STRABO. Ezra adds this from himself, who restored the whole library after the Babylonian captivity, all the books having been burned by Nebuchadnezzar; or Moses himself speaks of himself as of another.
7.1: 7.1 And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, I have appointed you the god, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 17 on Exodus, vol. 3. It is to be noted that when he was sent to the people, it was not said to him: Behold, I have made you God to the people, and your brother shall be your prophet; but, your brother shall speak to you to the people. It was also said, he shall be your mouth, and you shall be to him in the things that concern God; it was not said, you shall be God to him. But to Pharaoh Moses is said to be given as god, and by analogy Aaron is given as prophet to Moses, but toward Pharaoh. Here it is hinted to us that the prophets of God speak those things which they hear from him; and that a prophet of God is nothing else than an announcer of the words of God to men who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God. GREGORY, Hom. 8 on Ezekiel. Sometimes God is said by name only, sometimes essentially. By name, as here: I have appointed you god of Pharaoh. And elsewhere: Bring him to the gods. And elsewhere: God stood in the congregation of gods, etc. Essentially, as here: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, which Paul, wishing to distinguish, says: Of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God blessed above all forever. For God is said by name among all things, but essentially above all things; so, to show that Christ is God by nature, he recalled that he is not only God but God over all. For any just man is a god, but among all things, because by name: but Christ above all, because God by nature. AUGUSTINE, Question 18 on Exodus. God says constantly, etc., down to I will harden, that is, I will show how hard he is.
7.7: 7.7 Now Moses was eighty years old, etc. STRABO. On account of circumcision, namely, which was commanded to be celebrated on the eighth day: for the number eighty has the same signification as the number eight, which is less than it. Now Moses was eighty years old. When Moses and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh, Moses was eighty, and Aaron eighty-three: because the law, offered to the nations through preachers, taught spiritual circumcision, and they themselves strove to be perfectly cleansed, and thus preached the faith of the holy Trinity. Verse 9
7.10: 7.10 And Aaron took, etc. ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. 5. And he took the rod before Pharaoh, etc., down to: O death, I will be your death, etc. Which was turned into a serpent. The law of Moses was tasteless, as it were, like a rod, but turned into a serpent, that is, into spiritual understanding, it was made drinkable and delightful.
7.11: 7.11 And Pharaoh called the wise men, etc. It should be known that they either deluded the eyes of the onlookers with diabolical fabrications, so that things remaining in their own nature seemed otherwise; or, according to Augustine, demons, although evil, have not lost their nature: therefore while sorcerers try to effect something by their incantation, they run through the world and suddenly bring the seeds of those things which are in question. And so from these, God permitting, they produce new species of things. Likewise: in the first plague it says when the water is turned into blood; and in the second, when the frogs come up; and in the third, when the gnats swarm; in the fourth, when the dog-fly is brought forth; in the fifth, when the hand of the Lord is upon the cattle of the Egyptians, similar things are said.
7.12: 7.12 Serpents (dracones). They are so called from the Greek word for to see, because they see more sharply than other animals. But it devoured, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 21. If it had been said, The serpent of Aaron swallowed up their rods, it would be understood that the true serpent of Aaron had not swallowed up phantasmal fabrications but rods, etc., down to but God alone is the true creator, who has implanted in things their very causes and seminal principles.
7.13: 7.13 And hardened, etc. God hardened the heart of Pharaoh, because he so hardened the devil after sin that he is never softened by the compunction of repentance, as is said in Job 41: His heart shall be hardened like a stone.
7.15: 7.15 Go to him in the morning; behold he will go out, etc. ORIGEN, Hom. 4. At first Moses does not go in to Pharaoh, but meets him as he goes out to the waters; afterwards he does go in; after this he neither goes in, but being summoned approaches: because whether we are in a contest with Pharaoh in the word of God and the assertion of religion, or we try to rescue souls besieged by him, and there is a wrestling in us in disputation, we should not enter at the outset into the last places of the questions, but we must meet the adversary and at his waters, that is, the authorities of the Gentile philosophers, so as first to refute them and show that they have erred; then to go in to the inner parts of the contest. For the Lord says: Unless someone first binds the strong man, he cannot enter his house and plunder his goods (Mark 12 [sic]). First, then, the strong man must be bound and constrained with the bonds of questions, and so we must go in to plunder the vessels and free the souls which he had possessed by deceit and fraud. When we have done this many times, and stood against him, girt about the loins in truth, standing in the Lord and acting manfully, the ancient and cunning craftsman will pretend to be conquered and to yield, to make us more negligent for the contest. He will also feign repentance, he will beg us to depart, but not far: he wants us to be in some part neighbors to him. But unless we withdraw farther from him, and cross the sea, and say in thought, word and deed: As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us, we cannot be saved. Let us therefore pray for the mercy of God, that he may rescue us also from the land of Egypt, from the power of darkness, and sink Pharaoh with his army like lead in the mighty water. And we, set free, with joy and exultation let us sing a hymn to the Lord. For he has been gloriously honored, etc. ISIDORE. The plagues in Egypt were carried out bodily, but in us they are carried out spiritually. For Egypt is the form of the world.
7.17: 7.17 The water of the river, etc. STRABO. The water turned into blood signifies worldly wisdom, in which everyone who remains is killed, like a fish in blood. For worldly wisdom thinks it foolish that God should die for men; whoever therefore clings to this cannot live. ORIGEN. The water of the river is turned into blood, to which they had handed the boys of the Hebrews to be killed, so that for the authors of the crime it might return a cup of blood: and that in drinking they might feel the gore of the polluted flood, which they had stained with parricidal slaughter. Allegorically also the waters of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers, who deceived little ones in sense and understanding: but when the cross of Christ showed the light of truth, they are required to pay the penalty for the slaughter of their own and the guilt of blood. Hence: All the blood that has been shed upon the earth shall be required of this generation (Matt. 23).
7.20: 7.20 Which was turned into blood, etc. RABANUS. The first commandment, on worshipping one God: You shall have no other gods before me: the first plague, water turned into blood. Compare the first commandment to the first plague: water, from which all things are generated, signifies the one God, from whom are all things; blood, mortal flesh. The water was therefore turned into blood, because they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and this change takes place in the heart of the impious. Into blood, etc. Because those who in the causes of things think carnally are rebuked by such chastisements, that from the quality of the punishments they may recognize their error.
7.22: 7.22 And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened. AUGUSTINE, Question 22. It seems that the heart of Pharaoh was hardened for this reason, that the magicians of the Egyptians did similar things. But what follows teaches how great that hardening was, even when the magicians failed.
7.24: 7.24 And they dug, etc. Because the Gentile world, confounded by its meditation on secular philosophy, when it sees that there is nothing vital or wholesome in it, strives by searching on every side, seeking a draught of wisdom, and does not find it, until it comes to him who says: He who thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7).
8.2: 8.2 Behold, I will strike all your borders with frogs, etc. STRABO. There are three kinds of frogs: one of the river and vocal, another of the kind called calamita, of which it is said that if it is thrown into the mouth of a barking dog, it at once falls silent; the third of the kind called rubeta, because it lives in brambles. ORIGEN. Frogs signify the songs of the poets, who with empty and swollen modulation, like the sounds and songs of frogs, brought the fables of deception into the world: for that animal is useful for nothing, except that it gives out the sound of its voice in shameless and importunate cries. RABANUS. The second commandment: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. The name of God is truth: for he himself says: I am the truth. Whoever speaks the truth speaks of God; but whoever speaks a lie speaks of his own. For to speak the truth is to speak rationally: to speak vanity is to make a din. The second commandment, then, is about the love of truth, to which the love of iniquity is contrary. Truth speaks, vanity clamors. Contrary to this is the second plague, the abundance of frogs, whose loquacity signifies vanity. The lovers of truth do not take the name of God in vain, because they do not depart from truth into vanity. But those who contradict the truth, and, deceived by vanity, deceive, are frogs, bringing weariness to the ears, not food to the minds. Hear men speaking rationally, Psalm 18: There are no speeches nor words in which their voices are not heard. Hear the frogs: They have spoken vain things, every one to his neighbor, etc.
8.7: 8.7 And the magicians did also, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 23. It is asked from where, if it had already been done everywhere. But there is a similar question, from where they turned water into blood, if all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood? But it must be understood that the region where the children of Israel dwelt had not been struck by such plagues, and from there the magicians could draw water to turn into blood, or bring forth frogs for the display of magical power; although they could also do it after those plagues had been checked: but Scripture in narrating joined together what could be done afterwards.
8.10: 8.10 Who answered: Tomorrow. THEODORET. Pharaoh, wishing to know whether the prayers of Moses and Aaron had any power with God (for he supposed that they rested through the night), said: Tomorrow, so that he himself, going to the river, might see whether the frogs had ceased. Therefore God, that Moses might be believed, made the frogs cease not only at that very time which Moses had appointed, but ordered also those that were on the land to perish, lest they should think the same had returned.
8.15: 8.15 And Pharaoh seeing, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 24. Here it appears that Pharaoh was not hardened only because the magicians did similar things, etc., down to he did not say gifts, or rewards, but your judgments.
8.16: 8.16 Stretch out your rod, etc. Mystically. Moses chastising Egypt with the rod signifies the law, which rebukes the world with the ten plagues of the commandments. The rod also by which Egypt is corrected and Pharaoh overcome is the cross of Christ, by which the world is conquered and the devil overcome or triumphed over. The rod cast down becomes a serpent, which signifies wisdom, according to Matt. 10: Be wise as serpents, etc. The rod devoured the serpents of the magicians, and the cross of Christ, whose preaching seems foolishness, overcomes all the wisdom of the world. Hence: For he wrote of me (John 5). The rod cast on the ground was turned into a serpent, because when the mystery of the cross came to the faith of men, it made the wisdom of the world foolish. And let there be gnats, etc. ORIGEN. This animal is suspended on wings, flying through the air, but so subtle and minute that it escapes the sight unless one looks keenly. Yet when it has settled on the body, it pierces with a most bitter sting, so that one who cannot see it flying feels it stinging. This animal is therefore compared to the art of dialectic, which pierces souls with the minute and subtle stings of words, and goes around with such cunning that the one deceived neither sees nor understands whence he is deceived. RABANUS. Morally. The third commandment: Remember to sanctify the sabbath day. By this is hinted the rest and tranquillity of mind which a good conscience makes. There is sanctification, because there is the Spirit of God. Hence: Upon whom shall my Spirit rest but upon the humble and quiet? etc. (Isa. 66). The restless therefore recoil from the Holy Spirit, provokers of quarrels, lovers of calumnies, and do not admit the rest of the spiritual sabbath. Be gentle, then; let there be no tumult in your heart, with phantasms flitting through it in corruption and stinging you. Hear God saying, Psalm 45: Be still and see that I am God. You, through restlessness, are unwilling to be still, and blinded you demand to see what you cannot. Note the contrary plague: gnats were born in the land of Egypt from mud, minute and most restless flies, flying in disorder, rushing into the eyes, and denying men rest; when driven away they return; so are the phantasms of the restless. Hold the commandment, beware the plague.
8.18: 8.18 And there were gnats. Blood is the doctrine of the philosophers; frogs, the fictions of the poets; gnats, the sophisms of the dialecticians: all of which have deceived the world.
8.19: 8.19 This is the finger of God, etc. ISIDORE, from Augustine, ep. 119. At the third sign the magicians fail, saying: It is the finger of God: they had the type and the animosity of heretics. Hence: As Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith, etc. (2 Tim. 3). Those who through corruption of mind were restless failed at the third sign, confessing themselves opposed to the Holy Spirit, who was in Moses. For in the third place is put the Spirit, who is the finger of God: who as, when appeased, gives rest to the meek and humble of heart, so, when angered, disturbs the unmerciful and proud through restlessness, which the most grievous flies signified, under which the magicians failed, saying, This is the finger of God, lest they understand whence they are deceived. STRABO. It is to be noted that the magicians were conquered at the third sign, because all perfidy and worldly wisdom or philosophy is conquered by the faith of the Trinity. For when they discovered philosophy and disputed about the machinery of the whole world, they could not come to the knowledge of the Trinity. By the finger the Holy Spirit is understood, not because he is less than the Father and the Son, but because in the finger there are many divisions, and through the Holy Spirit the division of graces is given. AUGUSTINE, Question 25 on Exodus, vol. 3. What the magicians said to Pharaoh, etc., down to although they did not keep silent about the Son.
8.20: 8.20 Thus says the Lord, etc. RABANUS. The fourth commandment: Honor your father and your mother. Contrary to this is the fourth plague, namely the dog-fly, that is, the canine fly: it is canine not to recognize parents; hence their pups are born blind.
8.21: 8.21 All kinds of flies. ISIDORE. Mystically. In the fourth place Egypt is struck with flies. The fly is an insolent and restless animal, in which the insolent cares of carnal desires are figured. Egypt is struck with flies because the hearts of those who love the world are smitten with the restlessness of desires. The Septuagint put cynomyia, that is, the dog-fly: by which canine ways are signified, in which the pleasure of the human mind and the lust of the flesh are indicated. The eloquence of the law courts can also be signified by the dog-fly, of men who like dogs tear one another. PROCOPIUS. God does not use great beasts in overcoming Egypt, but calls on the service of the most contemptible little creatures and insects: lest the effect be ascribed to their power. To those abject and weak little creatures he gives unconquerable strength, so that Egypt despairs of being able to resist them, and cries out: This is the finger of God: for the whole world gathered together could not bear the hand of God. ORIGEN. The dog-fly is the sect of the heretics [other reading, of the Cynics], who, in addition to the other wickednesses of their deceit, preach pleasure and lust as the highest good. Since therefore the world was first deceived through each of these things, rightly the word and law of God, coming, rebukes with chastisements of this kind, so that from the quality of the punishments they may know the qualities of their own error.
8.22: 8.22 And I will make wonderful, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 26. It is to be understood that this was done in the earlier signs, that the land in which the people of God dwelt was not vexed with any such plagues. But it was opportune that it be openly stated here; from here signs now begin which the magicians did not try to imitate. For it is certain that gnats had been everywhere in the kingdom of Pharaoh, but had not been in the land of Goshen or Gesen: there the magicians tried to do similar things, and could not: until they failed, nothing was said about the separation of that land, but from the time that things began to happen which they did not even dare to attempt.
8.24: 8.24 And there came a very grievous swarm of flies, etc. AUGUSTINE, ibid. Fly is put for a multitude of flies. For I do not know how, through the custom of speech with which the minds of men are imbued, what is said in the singular often seems more than what is said in the plural; for example: There is a soldier there, rather than There are soldiers there; There is a fish there signifies more than There are fish there.
8.26: 8.26 Abominations. The perverse abominate the good things. The Egyptians, that is, the citizens of this world, abominate sheep, that is, the simplicity of the good. For as the good abominate evil things, so the wicked abominate good ones. Hence the good abominate the impious man, and the impious those who are in the right way. AUGUSTINE, Question 28. Moses said he wished to go into the wilderness where the Egyptians would not see their abominations. This must be understood as mystically signifying what we have said about shepherds, who were an abomination to the Egyptians: and therefore the Israelites received a separate land in Egypt. For so the sacrifices of the Israelites are abominations to the Egyptians, as the life of the just is to the unjust. STRABO. Historically. The Egyptians abominate sheep and yet adore them on account of Jupiter Ammon, who is depicted with a ram's head. Likewise: the Egyptians worship the ox, which is consecrated to Apis, as the cow to Isis. Apis was the greatest deity of the Egyptians, who appeared once a year at a fixed time to their priests. They, following him with hymns and praises, prophesied as if frenzied. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 18, ch. 28, vol. 2. Egypt is struck with flies, etc., down to Be still and see that I am God.
8.32: 8.32 And his heart was hardened, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 29. When the locust had been taken away, it was said of Pharaoh: Pharaoh hardened his heart even at this time, and would not let the people go. Surely now it was not said, The heart of Pharaoh was hardened, but Pharaoh hardened his own heart. So in all the plagues. The origin of vices is from the will of man. But the hearts of men are moved by causes, some in one way, some in another, even without different causes, often in a different manner, according to their own qualities, which come from their wills.
9.1: 9.1 And the Lord said to Moses, etc. PROCOPIUS. First among the beasts of burden are counted horses, which are liars or false as to salvation. Then the unclean beasts of burden, which neither part the hoof nor chew the cud, yet are yoked to the chariot. Next camels, which, although on account of rumination they are reckoned as it were clean, yet because their hoof is not cloven are accounted unclean. Nevertheless camels are said to be of partly clean, partly unclean condition. Furthermore, because this plague was believed to be little harmful on account of the vileness of unclean animals, it passes to oxen, then to the most gentle of animals, the sheep. ORIGEN, Hom. 4. In the fifth place Egypt is struck by the death of animals or cattle. In this the senselessness or folly of mortals is rebuked, who, as though they were irrational beasts, imposed the worship and name of God on figures, impressed not only on men but on beasts, in wood and stone: venerating Jupiter Ammon in a ram, Anubis in a dog, Apis in a bull, and the other monstrosities of gods which Egypt admires, so that in those things to which they believed divine worship was due they might see pitiable punishment. RABANUS, on Exodus, vol. 2. The fifth commandment is: You shall not commit adultery, etc., down to note the plague: if you are a beast, at least fear to die.
9.7: 9.7 And his heart was hardened, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 30. If the cattle of the Israelites had died, there would seem to be a suitable cause why his heart was hardened to contempt of God, as if his magicians had killed the cattle of the Israelites; but whence he ought to have been moved to fear or believe, he was hardened, and that hardening has even advanced thus far.
9.8: 9.8 Take full, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 31. Another reading: Take for yourselves full handfuls of ashes from the furnace, and Moses shall sprinkle, etc. The earlier signs were done with a rod, which not Moses but Aaron stretched out over the water or struck on the ground. But now, two signs having intervened, namely of the dog-fly and the deaths of the cattle, in which neither Aaron nor Moses does anything with the hand, it is said that Moses should sprinkle the ashes toward heaven; both are commanded to take them, but he to sprinkle not on the ground but toward heaven: as though Aaron, who had been given to the people, ought to strike the earth, or stretch out his hand upon the water or the land; but Moses, who was in the things that pertain to the Lord, is commanded to sprinkle the ashes. What of those two earlier signs, in which neither Moses nor Aaron does anything with the hand? What does this very diversity mean? For it is not nothing. RABANUS. The sixth commandment: You shall not kill; the sixth plague, pustules on the body, boiling and bursting blisters, the burning of wounds and the ashes of the furnace. For murderers burn with anger and madness. If you could see the souls of murderers, you would lament them more than the putrefying bodies of the ulcerated.
9.9: 9.9 ORIGEN, ibid. Wounds and blisters with heat are produced in the sixth stroke. In the ulcers deceitful and festering malice is rebuked; in the blisters, swelling and puffed-up pride; in the heat, anger and the madness of rage.
9.13: 9.13 And the Lord hardened the heart, etc. ORIGEN, ibid. Note that in the sixth plague it is not said, The heart of Pharaoh was hardened, but something more terrible is added; for it is written that the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, etc. Again, in the seventh, when hail and fire lay waste Egypt, the heart of Pharaoh is indeed hardened, but not by the Lord. In the eighth, however, where the locust is brought, the Lord is said to harden the heart of Pharaoh. And in the ninth, when the darkness becomes palpable, and finally when, the firstborn being slain, the Israelites had departed, it is said thus: And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt and of his servants, and he pursued them. But also when Moses is sent from the land of Midian to Egypt and commanded to do wonders, it is added: You shall do them in the sight of Pharaoh: but I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, etc. Hence it was first said by the Lord: I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, etc. A second time also, after the princes of Israel were enumerated, it is said: I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, etc. This variety was not made in vain, that now the Lord is said to have hardened the heart of Pharaoh, now that it was hardened of itself. I see Paul, as one who understood what the difference is, saying that the heart of Pharaoh was hardened and that the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, Rom. 2: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, and patience, and longsuffering? Do you not know that the benignity of God leads you to repentance, etc. Here without doubt he blames the one who was hardened of his own accord. But elsewhere, as though proposing a question on this, he says: Therefore he has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens, etc. He adds also to these: O man, who are you that reply to God? (Rom. 9). By which, concerning him who is said by the Lord to be hardened, he answers not so much by the solution of the question as by apostolic authority, according to the incapacity of the hearers, as he says elsewhere, 2 Cor. 12: And he heard secret words, which it is not granted to man to utter. Hence in what follows he deters the one who, not so much from merit of study as from a desire of knowing, plunges himself too curiously into more secret questions, saying, Rom. 9: O man, who are you that reply to God? RABANUS. The seventh commandment: You shall not steal; the seventh plague, hail on the fruits. For no one has unjust gain without just loss. While you steal, you acquire a garment, you lose faith: a visible gain, an invisible loss: gain from your blindness, loss from the cloud of the Lord. For those who steal outwardly from evil desire are hailed upon inwardly by judgment, and the field of their heart is laid waste.
9.16: 9.16 And therefore have I set you, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 32. The Apostle put these words, etc., down to for their benefit, therefore, Pharaoh was preserved.
9.18: 9.18 Behold, I will rain tomorrow, etc. ORIGEN. Thus far the punishments for the world are tempered through the figures of their own errors: after this come blows from above.
9.19: 9.19 Send therefore now, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 35 on Exodus, vol. 3. God seems to forewarn this not so much in indignation as in mercy, etc., down to since God threatened the death of the cattle, although Scripture was silent about it. PROCOPIUS. Moreover, it was by divine providence that not all the beasts of burden perished. For beasts of burden were needed to draw the chariots with which Pharaoh was afterwards to pursue the fugitives, to slaughter them in the wilderness. But divine providence governed the whole business otherwise.
9.22: 9.22 Stretch out your hand, etc. PROCOPIUS. The reader is to be reminded at this place that Moses is not commanded to do all the wonders with the rod, but at least some: some also to foretell, like the gnats and the death of the beasts of burden: some to be carried out by the ministry of the hands, as when he takes soot from the furnace and stirs up the hail. But what is the reason for this? Lest the crowd suppose that the rod was made by magical superstition, and ascribe those marvelous effects to it.
9.23: 9.23 And Moses stretched forth his rod, etc. ORIGEN, as above. This too must be noted, that some strokes Aaron is said to inflict on Pharaoh or Egypt, some Moses, and some the Lord himself. For in the first plague, where he turns the waters into blood, Aaron lifts the rod and strikes the water. In the second he strikes the waters and brings forth frogs. In the third he stretches out his hand and strikes with the rod the dust of the earth, and gnats are made. In the fourth the Lord is said to have made the dog-fly come. In the fifth also, when the cattle are destroyed, he is said to have done this word. In the sixth Moses sprinkles the ashes, and ulcers and blisters are made. In the seventh he lifts his hand to heaven and there are voices and hail, namely, etc. In the eighth likewise he stretches his hands to heaven, and the Lord brings a wind, and brings locusts. But in the ninth too he stretches his hand to heaven, and darkness and gloom are made. In the tenth the end and perfection of the whole work is administered by the Lord. For it is said: And the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt. THE SAME. Another difference is to be observed: in the first plague, when the water is turned into blood, it is not yet said to Moses that he should go in to Pharaoh, but, go to meet him, etc. In the second, the first having been constantly and faithfully carried out, it is said to him: Go in to Pharaoh, etc. In the third gnats are brought in, the magicians yield, confessing, This is the finger of God. In the fourth Moses is commanded to rise early and stand against Pharaoh as he comes out to the waters, when the houses of the Egyptians are filled with the dog-fly. In the fifth, when the cattle are destroyed, he is commanded to go in to Pharaoh. In the sixth Pharaoh is despised, and it is not said that Moses and Aaron went in to him, because ulcers and blisters with heat were made even upon the magicians, and they could not stand before Moses. In the seventh he is commanded to rise very early and stand against Pharaoh, when he brings hail and fire and voices. In the eighth he is commanded to go in to him when the locust is brought. In the ninth Pharaoh is again despised, and Moses is commanded to stretch out his hands to heaven, that palpable darkness may be made: and he does not go in, but is called to Pharaoh. Likewise in the tenth, when the firstborn are destroyed, and he is forced to go out of Egypt in haste. And the Lord sent thunder, etc. THE SAME, Hom. 4. See the tempering of divine correction: he does not strike in silence, but gives voices, and sends doctrine from heaven, by which the chastened world may recognize its fault. He gives hail, by which the tender and still-growing things of the vices are laid waste. He gives fire also, knowing there are thorns and briers which it must consume, of which the Lord says, Luke 12: I am come to cast fire on the earth. By this fire the incentives of pleasure and lust are consumed. THE SAME. There are many other things to be observed, in which divine wisdom is shown. First, Pharaoh is not bent when the water is turned into blood. In the second he seems to be softened a little: for he called Moses and Aaron, saying: Pray the Lord for me, etc. In the third the magicians yield, saying: This is the finger of God, etc. In the fourth, struck by the dog-fly, he says: Go and sacrifice to the Lord your God, etc. In the fifth, where the deaths of the cattle are mentioned, he does not yield, but hardened the more. Likewise in the sixth, over the plague of ulcers. In the seventh, when he is laid waste by hail and fires, he called Moses and Aaron, saying: I have sinned this time also; the Lord is just, but I and my people are wicked, etc. In the eighth, pressed by the locusts, he hastily called Moses and Aaron, saying: I have sinned against the Lord your God, and against you. Forgive my sin, and now pray to the Lord your God. In the ninth, when covered by darkness, he calls Moses and Aaron, saying: Go and serve the Lord your God. In the tenth, when the firstborn are destroyed, he calls them by night and says: Arise, go forth from among my people, you and the children of Israel, etc. And he adds: But bless me also. These things cannot be explained except by the same spirit by which they were done, because, according to the Apostle, 1 Cor. 14, the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets; so they are not said to be subject to just anyone for explaining the sayings of the prophets, but to the prophets.
9.30: 9.30 But I know that, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 35 on Exodus. Pharaoh had been terrified by the crashing of the sky and the hail. Hence he asked Moses to pray for him, confessing his iniquity and that of his people. But Moses was looking for another fear. For it is easy to fear punishment: but this is not to fear God, namely with that fear of piety of which Jacob says: Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, you would now have sent me away empty (Gen. 31).
10.1: 10.1 For I have hardened his heart, etc. AUGUSTINE, Question 36 on Exodus. He did not say this as though God had need of anyone's malice, but it must be understood as if he said: I have been patient with him and his servants, so as not to take them away, that my signs might come upon them in order; for because the evil mind became more obstinate through the patience of God, it is said, on account of my having been patient with him, I made his heart heavy. The plagues of the Egyptians are the instruction of the children of Israel, that they may not be hardened likewise and suffer the like. When the pestilent man is punished, the little one will be wiser. ORIGEN. The ten plagues with which Egypt is struck through the Israelites can be compared to the times of the Roman empire, because these things were done as a figure of us. The Christian people and the Israelite people belong to one God; one cause of each was subjected, the Synagogue to the Egyptians, the Church to the Romans. The Egyptians persecuted, the Romans persecuted too. There Moses is opposed ten times, here there are ten edicts against Christ. There were various plagues of the Egyptians, here various calamities of the Romans. There first blood flows from the wells and rivers; here the first plague under Nero, so that everywhere there was the blood of the dying, either corrupted by diseases in the City or poured out in wars in the world. There the second plague, frogs in the inner chambers, nearly destroyed the inhabitants with want of food: here under Domitian unbridled attendants, at the command of the bloody prince, and want, scattered nearly all the Roman citizens. There the third plague, gnats, most savage little flies, which in midsummer fly in swarms through squalid places and are borne upon the hair of men and the bristles of beasts with a burning bite: here the third plague under Trajan stirred up the Jews, who, having before been dispersed and quiet as though they did not exist, moved by sudden heat, ran riot. Besides, many cities fell in earthquake in the same times. There the fourth plague, dog-flies, nurslings of putrefaction, mothers of worms: here under Marcus Antoninus a pestilence poured over many provinces gave Italy and the city of Rome, and the army of the Romans scattered through various winter quarters, dissolved by death, to putrefaction and worms. There the fifth plague, of cattle and beasts of burden: here under the persecutor Severus in civil wars the very entrails and supports of the republic, that is, the plebs of the provinces and the legions of soldiers, were cut to pieces. There the sixth plague, swelling blisters and flowing ulcers: here the plague that followed the persecution of Maximinus, who specially commanded that bishops and clerics, passing over the popular crowd, the chiefs of the Churches, be tortured, swelling frequently with anger and perfidy, was raised not through slaughter of the common people but through the wounds of dying princes and powerful men. There the seventh plague, hail compacted in the air, which was destruction to men and beasts of burden: here under Gallus and Volusianus, who succeeded the persecutor Decius, a pestilence was poured through all the spaces of the Roman realm and gave almost every kind of mankind to death. There the eighth correction, locusts stirred up on every side: here nations stirred up on every side laid waste the Roman world with slaughter and fires. There the ninth plague, tangible darkness, threatening more danger than it caused: here, when the persecutor Aurelian was decreeing, a terrible thunderbolt fell with dire whirlwinds at his very feet, showing what so great an avenger would do were he not patient; although within six months three emperors were killed, Aurelian, Tacitus and Florian. There the tenth and last plague, the slaughter of the firstborn: here the destruction of all the idols, which the first things made they loved first. There the king proved, and felt, and feared the power of God, and let the people of God go free: here also he did all this, and even believed. THE SAME. There the people of God was not drawn back to servitude, nor here afterwards forced to idolatry. There the precious vessels of the Egyptians were handed to the Hebrews: here the precious temples of the pagans yielded to the Church of the Christians. THE SAME. As the Egyptians pursued the Hebrews, dismissed after the ten plagues, destruction of the sea rushed upon them: for us too, on pilgrimage, the persecution of the Gentiles remains, until we cross the Red Sea, that is the fire of judgment, with Christ as leader and judge. But those who persecute Christians, with their king Antichrist, will be sunk in the lake of eternal fire.
10.4: 10.4 Behold, I will bring in tomorrow the locust, etc. RABANUS. The eighth commandment: You shall not bear false witness: the eighth plague, locust, an animal, namely, harmful with its tooth. For a false witness harms by biting and consumes by lying. Hence: If you bite and devour one another, take heed that you be not consumed one of another (Gal. 5). ORIGEN, Hom. 4 on Exodus. I think by this kind of plague the inconstancy of the human race, always at variance and in discord with itself, is refuted. For the locust, though it has no king, according to Scripture, leads its army in order: but men, when made rational, neither could rule themselves in order, nor patiently bore the governance of God who rules. STRABO. By the locust, which has no king, is signified the rashness of those who, although smitten with various punishments, always remain in their hardness as though they had no ruler. Locust. ISIDORE. Locusts are taken for the mobility of levity, like wandering and leaping souls after the pleasure of the world.
10.13: 10.13 And Moses stretched forth his rod. RABANUS. Some wonders are done through Moses, some through Aaron, some through the Lord himself; that we may know that in some matters we are to be purged by the sacrifices of the priests and the supplications of the pontiffs, whom the person of Aaron designates: in others to be amended by knowledge of the law, which the office of Moses designates. In the more difficult matters, however, we need the power of the Lord himself. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 31, ch. 20. The plagues of Egypt, sent from heaven, etc., down to when with vain praises they enervate the works of certain persons now regarded as, so to speak, strong.
10.19: 10.19 There remained not one, etc. AUGUSTINE. Scripture certainly recorded the benefit of God, that he took away the locusts, and went on to say that the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, namely by his benefit and patience, by which he became more obstinate while he was spared: as all wicked hearts of men grow hard by misusing the patience of God.
10.21: 10.21 Stretch out your hand, etc. AUGUSTINE. A third time it is said to Moses: Stretch out your hand to heaven, that there may be also a plague of darkness. But it was never said to Aaron that he should stretch out his hands to heaven. As to what was said to Moses: Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, and let the locust come up upon the land, I believe it is signified that he who can do more can also do less; but not that he to whom lesser things are granted can at once do greater. ORIGEN. The ninth plague is darkness, that the blindness of their mind may be rebuked, or that they may understand that the reasons of divine dispensation and providence are most obscure. For God made darkness his hiding place (Ps. 17): which they, boldly and rashly searching into and asserting one thing after another, have fallen into the thick and palpable darkness of errors. STRABO. By the darkness is shown the folly of those [the Jews] who were afflicted and did not know to what end their punishments would come. Or also by the darkness is signified the secret of the divine judgment, by which he mercifully saves the just and justly condemns the impious.
10.24: 10.24 Only your sheep, etc. AUGUSTINE, in Expressions in Exodus, bk. 52 [sic]. The Greek has, apart from the sheep and the oxen, leave behind, and it is an unusual expression unless, after a pause, leave is inserted; and understand, those things, so that the sense is: Go, apart from the sheep and oxen, and leave those things. For such an ellipsis often occurs in the expressions of the Scriptures. RABANUS. The ninth commandment: You shall not covet your neighbor's wife: the ninth plague, thick darkness. For there is a kind of adultery even in desiring another's wife, when one's own does not suffice for someone, to tempt even another's. Truly the darkness is thick; for nothing so pains the one suffering, nothing would the doer so little wish to suffer: whoever does this is truly blinded by horrible madness.
